# The Attack on ISD (Gordon & Zemke, 2000)


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

## Summary
Gordon and Zemke's provocative Training magazine article launched a significant debate in the instructional design field by arguing that ISD (Instructional Systems Design) is flawed, out-of-date, and an obstacle to effective performance improvement. The authors contend that the ADDIE model is too slow, too rigid, and too focused on instructional solutions when non-instructional solutions are often more effective. The article catalyzed a years-long professional debate about whether ISD should be reformed or replaced, with responses appearing in subsequent issues and spawning the "attack on ISD" controversy in the field.

## Key Concepts
- ISD (Instructional Systems Design) critique
- ADDIE model limitations
- Rapid instructional design
- Non-instructional performance interventions
- HPT (Human Performance Technology) as ISD alternative

## Theoretical Framework
Practitioner critique of dominant paradigm; draws on practitioner experience and HPT principles to argue that academic ID models have failed to keep pace with organizational reality.

## Methods
Opinion/perspective piece combining practitioner experience, case examples, and selective literature review; published as a provocation intended to generate professional debate.

## Main Arguments
- ISD is too slow for modern organizational needs; the typical development timeline is incompatible with business timelines
- ADDIE's linear structure makes it unsuitable for real-world projects where analysis, design, and development overlap
- Many performance problems called "training needs" are actually organizational, motivational, or environmental in nature
- The field's attachment to ISD prevents adoption of more effective, agile approaches

## Limitations & Critiques
Critics argued Gordon and Zemke overstated the limitations of ISD by attacking a strawman version of the model; defenders noted that ISD, properly applied, is iterative and flexible; the article's provocative framing generated more heat than light in the subsequent debate.

# User Experience Design Professionals' Perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence


## Abstract
Among creative professionals, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has sparked excitement over its capabilities and fear over unanticipated consequences. How does GenAI impact User Experience Design (UXD) practice, and are fears warranted? We interviewed 20 UX Designers, with diverse experience and across companies (startups to large enterprises). We probed them to characterize their practices, and sample their attitudes, concerns, and expectations. We found that experienced designers are confident in their originality, creativity, and empathic skills, and find GenAI’s role as assistive. They emphasized the unique human factors of “enjoyment” and “agency”, where humans remain the arbiters of “AI alignment’’. However, skill degradation, job replacement, and creativity exhaustion can adversely impact junior designers. We discuss implications for human-GenAI collaboration, specifically copyright and ownership, human creativity and agency, and AI literacy and access. Through the lens of responsible and participatory AI, we contribute a deeper understanding of GenAI fears and opportunities for UXD.

**DOI:** [10.1145/3613904.3642114](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642114)

## Summary
This study examines UX design professionals' perceptions of generative AI tools, documenting how practitioners across industry and agency contexts understand, evaluate, and integrate (or resist) AI in their UX workflows. Through interviews with practicing UX designers and researchers, the paper maps attitudes along dimensions of trust, skill relevance, and professional identity. Findings reveal significant heterogeneity: some practitioners see AI as a powerful collaborator that amplifies their judgment; others view it as a threat to the tacit knowledge that defines professional expertise. The paper calls for UX education and professional development to address AI integration head-on.

- Professional identity and AI displacement anxiety

## Theoretical Framework
Professional cognition and expertise theory; technology acceptance model; human-AI collaboration framework; draws on UX practice literature and AI adoption research.

Semi-structured interviews with UX design professionals across roles (designer, researcher, content strategist); thematic analysis of perceptions, adoption patterns, and resistance motivations.

## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

## Summary
This paper explores industrial and UX designers' use of generative AI tools through the metaphor of "clay to play with" — positioning AI as a malleable, generative material that enables exploratory, low-stakes design experimentation. Through design research with practitioners in product and experience design contexts, the authors find that successful AI integration occurs when designers approach tools playfully and experimentally rather than instrumentally, treating AI outputs as starting points for design exploration rather than finished products. The paper argues for a materials-centered approach to understanding AI in design practice.

## Key Concepts
- AI as design material (not just a productivity tool)
- Playful and exploratory AI use
- Material encounters in design practice
- Generative AI in industrial design
- Experimentation and serendipity with AI

## Theoretical Framework
Material-centered design practice theory; draws on Ingold's material agency, Schön's reflective practice, and design studio research to frame AI as a new design material rather than a software tool.

## Methods
Design research with UX and industrial design practitioners; qualitative study combining design workshops, observation, and reflective interviews about AI material practice.

## Main Arguments
- Treating AI as a design material — something to manipulate, resist, and explore — produces richer outcomes than treating it as a productivity tool
- Playful experimentation with AI generates serendipitous discoveries that instrumentally-minded use misses
- The "clay" metaphor captures both the formability of AI outputs and the skill required to shape them toward design intent
- Design education should develop AI material literacy: understanding what this material can and cannot do, and how to develop craft with it

## Limitations & Critiques
The materials metaphor is productive but may not scale to all design contexts; the study's practitioner sample may represent early adopters; empirical evidence for learning outcomes from materials-based AI pedagogy is not yet established.

## Summary
This paper investigates how conversational AI assistants can support UX evaluation activities, examining what kinds of questions UX practitioners ask AI systems during evaluations and which question forms elicit useful responses. Through user studies with UX practitioners conducting AI-assisted evaluations, the authors identify categories of productive questions (heuristic interpretation, guideline application, pattern recognition) and unproductive ones (requiring contextual judgment, stakeholder knowledge, or domain-specific nuance). The paper provides practical guidance for UX practitioners integrating conversational AI into evaluation workflows.

- Conversational AI for UX evaluation
- Question formulation and prompt design for UX
- Heuristic evaluation with AI assistance
- AI limitations in contextual judgment tasks
- UX evaluation workflow AI integration

## Theoretical Framework
Cognitive task analysis of UX evaluation; human-AI collaboration in professional practice; usability evaluation methods; draws on Nielsen's heuristic evaluation and AI-assisted work literature.

## Methods
User studies with UX practitioners conducting heuristic evaluations with AI assistance; think-aloud protocols; analysis of question types and response quality; qualitative coding of AI interaction patterns.

## Main Arguments
- AI assistants are most useful for UX evaluation when practitioners ask questions that can be answered from general UX knowledge (heuristics, principles, patterns)
- Questions requiring contextual knowledge about users, business constraints, or organizational culture produce unreliable AI responses
- Effective AI-assisted UX evaluation requires practitioners to develop new prompt literacy skills specific to evaluation tasks
- AI assistance is best positioned as a first-pass tool that practitioners then refine using domain expertise and contextual knowledge

Study uses specific AI tools at a point in time; results may change as AI capabilities evolve; the sample of UX practitioners may skew toward those already comfortable with AI; evaluation contexts studied may not represent the full range of UX evaluation types.

# A Comparative Analysis

## Summary
Chapter 10 of Fitzpatrick, Sanders, and Worthen's *Program Evaluation: Alternative Approaches and Practical Guidelines* synthesizes the major evaluation traditions into a comparative framework organized into four categories: (1) expertise- and consumer-oriented approaches (judging overall quality), (2) approaches oriented to program characteristics, (3) decision-oriented approaches, and (4) participant-oriented approaches. The authors identify the conceptual contributions, methodological strengths, and contextual limitations of each tradition, arguing that no single approach is universally superior.

## Key Concepts
- **Expertise-oriented evaluation**: Expert judgment as the primary evaluation mechanism (e.g., accreditation models)
- **Consumer-oriented evaluation**: Evaluation to serve end-users and clients (Scriven's Consumer Reports model)
- **Decision-oriented evaluation**: Evaluation designed to inform specific decisions (CIPP model)
- **Participant-oriented evaluation**: Responsive and naturalistic approaches centering stakeholder voices
- **Methodological pluralism**: No single evaluation model is appropriate for all contexts

## Theoretical Framework
Comparative meta-evaluation. Synthesizes the conceptual foundations of major evaluation schools and assesses their practical utility across different evaluation purposes and contexts.

## Methods
Literature synthesis and expert analysis. Organizes existing evaluation frameworks into a typology and compares them across criteria: theoretical assumptions, methods, stakeholder orientation, and practical applicability.

## Main Arguments
1. Different evaluation purposes require different approaches; using only one model risks systematic blind spots
2. The four categories represent fundamentally different epistemological commitments and stakeholder orientations
3. Evaluators must be methodologically pluralistic, selecting approaches based on context
4. Understanding the conceptual roots of each approach is prerequisite to competent evaluation practice

## Limitations
Comparative framework inevitably simplifies complex traditions that differ internally; categorization schemes are analytical tools, not rigid taxonomies. The field has continued evolving since publication.

- Companion to [[Program Evaluation]] (Fitzpatrick et al. Ch. 1, textbook introduction)
- Relates to [[EVALUATING]] (Kirkpatrick as a decision-oriented evaluation approach)
- Connects to [[Kirkpatrick Plus Evaluation and Continuous]] on extending evaluation frameworks

# A Formative Study to Explore the Design of Generative UI Tools

## Summary
This formative study examines how generative UI (GenUI) tools — AI systems that produce UI code or mockups from natural language or design intent descriptions — can better support UX practitioners' workflows. Through a needs-finding study with UX practitioners across roles, the authors identify key gaps between current GenUI capabilities and professional UX practice requirements. The findings inform a set of design requirements for next-generation GenUI tools that account for the full complexity of professional UX work, not just rapid prototype generation.

## Key Concepts
- Generative UI (GenUI) tools for UX practice
- Needs-finding for GenUI tool design
- UX practitioner workflow requirements
- Gap between GenUI capabilities and professional use
- Design requirements for AI-assisted UI generation

## Theoretical Framework
User-centered design; needs-finding methodology; human-computer interaction; draws on design research methods and UX practice literature.

## Methods
Formative needs-finding study; semi-structured interviews and contextual inquiry with UX practitioners; qualitative analysis of workflow requirements and GenUI tool gaps.

## Main Arguments
- Current GenUI tools are designed for rapid individual prototyping but miss the iterative, collaborative, and specification-heavy dimensions of professional UX work
- UX practitioners need GenUI tools that support design system integration, accessibility checking, and design rationale communication, not just visual output
- The gap between GenUI capabilities and professional needs is a design opportunity requiring practitioner input throughout tool development
- Effective GenUI tools must accommodate different UX roles (designer, researcher, developer) with role-appropriate interfaces and outputs

## Limitations & Critiques
Needs-finding study informs design requirements but does not evaluate specific implementations; practitioner sample may not represent all UX contexts; the formative nature means requirements will evolve as GenUI technology advances.

# Accelerating Innovation with GenAI: Digital Prototyping (Bilgram and Laarmann)

## Summary
Bilgram and Laarmann report on six months of intensive experimentation with LLMs (especially GPT) in commercial innovation projects, demonstrating concrete use cases across the early innovation phases: exploration (need identification, trend analysis), ideation (idea generation, concept development), and digital prototyping (text-to-code generation for UX/UI). They argue that generative AI is democratizing prototyping by enabling non-technical team members to generate functional digital prototypes through natural language, collapsing the gap between concept and implementation in early innovation stages.

## Key Concepts
- AI-augmented innovation management
- LLM-enabled digital prototyping (text-to-code)
- Democratization of prototyping
- Early innovation phases (exploration, ideation, prototyping)
- No-code/low-code AI-assisted development

## Theoretical Framework
Practitioner-oriented; draws on innovation management literature and design thinking methodology; positions LLMs as general-purpose technologies applicable across the innovation front-end without requiring specialized technical expertise.

## Methods
Practitioner report; six months of experimental application of LLMs in internal and client-facing innovation projects; concrete use case documentation; reflection on team dynamics and AI-human interaction patterns.

## Main Arguments
- LLMs have crossed a threshold where they provide genuine value in creative and generative innovation tasks — previously thought to be human-only domains
- Text-to-code generation is the most transformative capability for non-technical innovators: it enables functional prototype creation without software skills, accelerating iteration dramatically
- Human-AI innovation teams require deliberate design: prompting, iteration, and quality evaluation are new skills that innovation teams must develop
- LLMs excel at divergent generation but require human judgment for convergent selection and quality assessment — the human role shifts from generation to curation and direction

## Limitations
- Based on a small innovation consultancy's experience; generalizability to larger organizations with different constraints is uncertain
- Published in 2023 based on GPT-3/4-era tools; capabilities have advanced significantly since, making specific claims about limitations or capabilities partially dated

## Connections
Relates to [[Vibe Coding for Product Design (Li et al.)]] on AI-assisted design and prototyping; links to [[Formative Study on GenUI Tools (Chen et al. Google DeepMind)]] on AI prototyping tools; connects to [[Anatomy of Prototypes (Lim Stolterman Tenenberg)]] on prototyping in design.

# Accelerating Innovation With

## Summary
This paper examines how generative AI tools are accelerating innovation workflows through AI-augmented digital prototyping and innovation methods, arguing that GenAI represents a qualitative shift in innovation capacity by compressing the ideation-to-prototype cycle. The authors present case studies of organizations using GenAI in early-stage innovation, documenting how AI-augmented digital prototyping enables rapid exploration of a wider solution space than traditional methods allow. The paper argues for a new "AI-augmented innovation" methodology that systematically integrates GenAI into established innovation frameworks.

## Key Concepts
- AI-augmented digital prototyping
- Innovation acceleration with GenAI
- Rapid solution space exploration
- AI-augmented innovation methodology
- Integration of GenAI into innovation frameworks

## Theoretical Framework
Innovation management; design thinking; human-AI collaboration; draws on innovation process research and emerging GenAI in design literature to frame the acceleration dynamic.

## Methods
Case studies of organizations using GenAI tools in digital prototyping and innovation workflows; qualitative analysis of workflow changes, speed improvements, and quality outcomes.

## Main Arguments
- GenAI compresses the ideation-to-prototype cycle in ways that enable wider solution space exploration without proportional time cost
- AI-augmented prototyping produces more diverse initial concepts than traditional brainstorming, though concept quality requires human curation
- Innovation teams need new workflows and competencies to benefit from GenAI acceleration rather than simply using it to do the same work faster
- The methodology requires integrating GenAI as a structural element of innovation process, not an ad hoc speed hack

## Limitations & Critiques
Case study evidence; GenAI innovation acceleration effects may be context-specific and depend on organizational readiness; the quality of AI-generated concepts is difficult to assess without long-term outcome tracking.

# Activity Theory for Workplace Learning Technologies (Martinez Marroquin and Senadji)

## Summary
Martinez Marroquin and Senadji apply Activity Theory as a framework for analyzing and designing workplace learning technologies, arguing that Engeström's expansive learning model provides a more robust account of technology-mediated workplace learning than cognitive models alone. The paper demonstrates how Activity Theory's components — subjects, tools, objects, rules, community, and division of labor — can inform the design of learning systems that account for the social, organizational, and contradictory dimensions of workplace learning. The work connects Vygotskian activity theory to contemporary learning technology design practice.

## Key Concepts
- Activity Theory (Vygotsky, Leont'ev, Engeström)
- Expansive learning
- Contradictions in activity systems
- Workplace learning technology design
- Sociocultural dimensions of technology-mediated learning

## Theoretical Framework
Activity Theory (third generation, Engeström); draws on cultural-historical psychology and organizational learning to provide an alternative to cognitive processing models of workplace learning.

## Methods
Conceptual framework application; case analysis of workplace learning technology design using Activity Theory as analytical lens; theoretical synthesis rather than primary empirical study.

## Main Arguments
- Cognitive approaches to learning technology design miss the social, organizational, and contradictory dimensions of workplace learning
- Activity Theory provides a holistic framework that accounts for how tools, rules, community, and division of labor shape learning
- Contradictions within and between activity systems are the primary driver of learning and innovation — technology design should surface rather than suppress them
- Workplace learning technology designers need frameworks that account for organizational context, not just individual learner cognition

## Limitations & Critiques
Activity Theory is complex and can be difficult to operationalize in design practice; the framework's Marxist roots create translation challenges in some organizational contexts; the application to technology design requires significant conceptual work.

# AECT Definition and Terminology (2008)

## Summary
The 2008 AECT Definition and Terminology Committee chapter presents the field's official redefinition of educational technology: "the study and ethical practice of facilitating learning and improving performance by creating, using, and managing appropriate technological processes and resources." The definition explicitly adds "ethical practice" and frames educational technology as both a field of study (theoretical) and a field of practice, emphasizing five key functions: creating, using, managing, learning, and performance.

## Key Concepts
- **Educational Technology**: Study and ethical practice of facilitating learning and improving performance
- **Creating**: Theory and practice of generating instructional materials and environments
- **Using**: Theory and practice of bringing learners into contact with instructional materials
- **Managing**: Organizational and leadership functions within the field
- **Performance**: Application of knowledge and skills to improve capability, distinct from learning

## Theoretical Framework
Builds on prior AECT definitions (1977, 1994) while responding to shifts in the field away from hardware-focused conceptions toward process, performance, and ethics. The 2008 definition explicitly incorporates ethics—absent in prior definitions—reflecting growing attention to responsible practice.

## Methods
Committee-based definitional work through literature synthesis and expert deliberation. Each term in the definition is elaborated with theoretical and practical grounding.

## Main Arguments
1. Educational technology cannot be reduced to equipment or media; it encompasses study and practice
2. "Ethical practice" is a constitutive element, not an add-on, reflecting responsibility to learners and society
3. The field spans multiple functions (creating, using, managing) rather than any single activity
4. Performance—not just learning—is a legitimate and distinct goal of educational technology practice

## Limitations
Definitional work is inherently contested; critics argue the 2008 definition is too broad to be distinctive or operationalizable. The committee process reflects a particular scholarly community's priorities. See Lowenthal & Wilson (2010) for critique.

# AI and Work Transformations: Sensemaking Perspectives (Engstrom et al. Jonkoping)

## Summary
Engström et al. explore how organizational members make initial sense of AI adoption in their workplaces and how this sensemaking shapes workplace learning trajectories. Through 23 focus groups at four large Swedish manufacturing companies, they find that sensemaking triggered by abstract AI features (AI as intelligent, autonomous) tends toward exploitative learning (refining existing practices), while sensemaking triggered by concrete AI features (AI as a specific tool) tends toward explorative learning paths (discovering new approaches). Socio-technical processes are crucial for the explorative path.

## Key Concepts
- Sensemaking theory (Weick)
- Initial sensemaking of AI adoption
- Exploitative vs. explorative workplace learning
- Abstract vs. concrete features of AI technologies
- Socio-technical learning processes

## Theoretical Framework
Combines Weick's sensemaking theory with organizational learning theory (exploitation/exploration dichotomy, March); frames AI adoption as a sensemaking process that precedes and shapes learning trajectories; draws on sociotechnical systems theory for analysis of enabling conditions.

## Methods
Qualitative, explorative, and interactive; 23 focus groups across four large Swedish manufacturing organizations; Gioia method for data analysis; two aggregated sensemaking dimensions derived inductively.

## Main Arguments
- Workers' initial mental models of AI (abstract vs. concrete) systematically predict learning trajectories — abstract anthropomorphic conceptions push toward incremental exploitation; concrete tool conceptions enable genuine exploration
- Organizations must attend to sensemaking processes during AI adoption, not just implementation logistics — wrong sensemaking channels learning in sub-optimal directions
- Socio-technical configurations (how work is organized around AI, who collaborates with whom) are more influential than the AI technology itself in determining learning outcomes
- This is one of the first studies to empirically connect sensemaking to workplace learning modes in AI adoption contexts

## Limitations
- Swedish manufacturing context; sensemaking dynamics may differ significantly in service industries, knowledge work, or non-Nordic organizational cultures
- Focus group data captures expressed sensemaking but may not fully reflect tacit assumptions guiding behavior

## Connections
Relates to [[Activity Theory for Workplace Learning Technologies (Martinez Marroquin and Senadji)]] on technology and workplace learning; links to [[Learning from Notes Groupware Implementation (Orlikowski 2002)]] on organizational sensemaking and technology; connects to [[Designing Job Characteristics for Hybrid Intelligence (Yang and Jiang)]] on AI-integrated work design.

# AI Assistance in Enterprise UX Workflows (Zhu et al. Kookmin)

## Summary
Zhu, Lee, Pan, and Cai examine how AI tools — specifically ChatGPT — affect designers' workflows in corporate enterprise environments, focusing on the creation and evaluation of design briefs. Through expert interviews, experimental testing, and third-party evaluations, they find that AI significantly enhances operational efficiency and subjective experience across most tasks: supporting information retrieval, analysis, communication, and decision-making. However, challenges remain around information authenticity, copyright, and professional identity maintenance. The paper advocates for human-centric AI integration frameworks.

## Key Concepts
- AI-assisted design brief creation
- Enterprise UX workflow
- AI thinking integration
- Human-centric AI in corporate design
- Professional identity and AI tools

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on human-computer interaction research, design management theory, and UX workflow analysis; uses user experience mapping as an analytical tool to compare pre/post AI integration experiences.

## Methods
Mixed methods: expert interviews with designers, experimental testing of ChatGPT in design brief tasks, and third-party expert evaluations of output quality; UX map visualization of the testing process.

## Main Arguments
- AI tools provide genuine operational value in enterprise UX contexts, particularly for information-intensive phases like brief creation, where domain gaps and communication complexity create friction
- Designers' subjective experience of AI assistance is largely positive, but concerns about accuracy and authenticity require ongoing critical engagement with AI outputs
- Professional identity challenges arise when designers feel AI encroaches on their expert judgment — organizations must manage this through cultural norms and training
- Effective integration requires designers to develop "AI thinking": understanding what AI does well and structuring workflows to leverage it appropriately

## Limitations
- Single institution study (Kookmin University, Seoul); enterprise contexts vary significantly in tools, norms, and design brief complexity
- Focus on brief creation is a narrow slice of full UX workflow; findings may not generalize to later design phases requiring more tacit judgment

# AI Failure Loops in Devalued Work (Kawakami et al.)

## Summary
Kawakami et al. conceptualize "AI Failure Loops" — self-reinforcing sociotechnical failures that occur when workplace AI is deployed in feminized labor contexts (social work, K-12 teaching, home healthcare) where worker expertise is systematically devalued. The paper argues that overconfidence in AI capabilities and underconfidence in worker expertise compound each other, producing AI systems that fail to enhance labor and further erode workers' visibility. Understanding occupational devaluation is essential to diagnosing why workplace AI so consistently disappoints.

## Key Concepts
- AI Failure Loops (interwoven sociotechnical failure modes)
- Feminized labor (historically devalued care/service occupations)
- Occupational devaluation
- Cognitive offloading and worker expertise erosion
- AI governance and evaluation failures

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on Science and Technology Studies (STS), organizational sociology of labor, and HCI literature on AI deployment failures, centering the concept of occupational devaluation as the explanatory mechanism that prior AI failure accounts have overlooked.

## Methods
Focused literature review of academic and grey literature on AI deployments in three feminized labor domains in the US (K-12 education, home healthcare, social work), synthesized through a conceptual framework-building approach.

## Main Arguments
- Worker expertise devaluation shapes AI design assumptions, creating systems that fail to capture or support tacit knowledge
- AI Failure Loops are cyclical: poor AI design → reduced trust → reduced use → further devaluation of worker input → worse AI design
- Three case domains show consistent patterns of AI tools that add burden, reduce autonomy, and are ultimately withdrawn or ignored
- Responsible AI governance must explicitly account for labor power dynamics and occupational status

## Limitations & Critiques
The review is confined to US feminized labor contexts, limiting generalizability, and does not include primary empirical data from workers themselves, relying instead on synthesized prior literature.

## Summary
Xiao et al. conduct a longitudinal study (2023–2025) of a software development organization, finding that AI tools substantially boosted individual productivity but failed to improve — and in some ways complicated — collaborative teamwork. Rather than fixing coordination and communication challenges, AI shifted the collaborative culture: increasing individual autonomy, reducing interdependence, and changing how teams communicate about work. The study is important for challenging the assumption that productivity gains at the individual level automatically improve collective performance.

## Key Concepts
- AI and teamwork in software development
- Individual vs. collective productivity under AI
- Collaborative culture shift (not improvement)
- Longitudinal organizational study methodology

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on CSCW and organizational behavior literature on AI and collaboration; longitudinal naturalistic study design tracks change over time rather than snapshot measurement.

## Methods
Longitudinal study (2023–2025) of a project-based software development organization; mixed methods combining quantitative productivity metrics with qualitative cultural analysis; multi-institution team (CMU, MIT, Stanford, Emory/Penn).

## Main Arguments
- AI tools boosted individual productivity but did not fix team coordination problems
- AI shifted collaborative culture by increasing individual autonomy and reducing interdependence
- The assumption that individual productivity gains translate to team gains is empirically unsupported
- Organizations need team-level AI adoption strategies, not just individual tool deployment

# AI Hasnt Fixed Teamwork Longitudinal Study (CMU MIT Stanford Emory)

## Summary
Xiao et al. conduct a two-wave longitudinal interview study (2023-2025) with 15 members of a project-based software development organization, tracking how expectations about AI's role in teamwork evolved after ChatGPT's release. Initial optimism that AI would coordinate projects and ease interpersonal friction gave way to a more limited reality: by 2025, AI was used mainly to accelerate individual tasks (coding, writing, documentation), leaving persistent collaboration challenges (performance accountability, fragile communication) unresolved. Yet AI did reshape collaborative culture — efficiency became a norm, responsible AI use became a marker of professionalism.

## Key Concepts
- AI in teamwork and collaboration
- Longitudinal study of AI adoption
- Individual productivity vs. team coordination AI
- Collaborative culture shift
- AI as performance accountability mediator

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on CSCW, organizational behavior, and human-AI interaction literature; frames AI in teams through the lens of sociotechnical systems — expecting technology to solve fundamentally social coordination problems leads to disappointment, while cultural shifts emerge as unexpected consequences.

## Methods
Longitudinal two-wave qualitative interview study (Wave 1: early 2023, N=15; Wave 2: 2025, same organization); thematic analysis of interview transcripts tracking expectation evolution and behavioral change over the two-year period.

## Main Arguments
- AI has dramatically boosted individual productivity in software development but has not touched the core social challenges of teamwork: trust, accountability, communication norms
- Early AI hype in organizational contexts created inflated expectations for AI as "intelligent coordinator" — expectations that were not met, creating disillusionment alongside genuine productivity gains
- AI's actual impact on teamwork is cultural: it shifted norms around efficiency expectations, transparency, and what counts as responsible contribution — changes that are significant but different from the predicted coordination transformation
- The individual/team productivity gap in AI adoption may be widening — individual workers become more capable while team coordination remains static

## Limitations
- Single organization case study; software development culture may not generalize to other knowledge work contexts
- Small longitudinal sample (N=15) limits statistical power for documenting cultural shifts; findings are qualitative and suggestive

# AI Hasn’t Fixed Teamwork, But It Shifted Collaborative


## Abstract
When AI entered the workplace, many believed it could re- shape teamwork as profoundly as it boosted individual pro- ductivity. Wo

## Summary
This paper examines how AI tools have changed collaborative dynamics in professional teams, arguing that while AI has not solved fundamental teamwork challenges (coordination, communication, trust), it has shifted where and how those challenges manifest. Through case studies and interviews with teams using AI tools, the authors document how AI changes the distribution of work within teams, the nature of handoffs, and the skills required for effective collaboration. The paper identifies new collaboration competencies required in AI-mediated team contexts.

## Key Concepts
- AI and team collaboration dynamics
- Work redistribution in AI-augmented teams
- Handoff challenges in human-AI-human workflows
- New collaboration competencies for AI-mediated work
- Trust and communication in AI-assisted teamwork

## Theoretical Framework
CSCW (Computer-Supported Cooperative Work); team cognition; human-AI teaming; draws on distributed cognition and coordination theory to analyze AI effects on team dynamics.

## Methods
Case studies of professional teams using AI tools; qualitative interviews with team members; observation of AI-mediated collaboration sessions; analysis of coordination patterns.

## Main Arguments
- AI tools shift where collaboration challenges occur rather than eliminating them: new friction points emerge around AI output evaluation and integration
- Teams develop new handoff practices for AI-generated outputs that require new competencies in quality assessment and contextual appropriateness evaluation
- Trust in AI varies within teams, creating asymmetric human-AI relationships that affect team coordination
- Effective AI-augmented teams develop shared norms around AI use that individual AI adoption cannot achieve

## Limitations & Critiques
Case study design limits generalizability; team AI tool use is rapidly evolving; the specific tools studied may not represent the landscape broadly; long-term effects on team collaboration culture are not tracked.

# AI Imaginaries: A Historical Timeline

> *A synthesis note drawing on vault papers and Adam Prumm's literature review "AI Imaginaries, Design Education, and the Transformation of Design Practice" (2025, unpublished).*

---

## What Is an Imaginary?

A **sociotechnical imaginary** is a collectively held vision of a desirable (or feared) social future made possible by a technology — visions that shape decisions, resource allocation, and policy *before* the technology matures. Jasanoff & Kim's foundational concept describes these as "collectively imagined forms of social life and social order reflected in the design and fulfillment of nation-specific scientific and/or technological projects."

Mager & Katzenbach (2021) sharpen this: imaginaries are **"multiple, contested, and commodified narratives"** — not neutral predictions, but political acts. They carry **performative power**: once an imagined future gains institutional momentum, it begins directing real priorities and behaviors regardless of whether it ever arrives. Stanusch et al. (2024) call these failures **"underperforming imaginaries"** — expected AI transformations that never materialize but still *reshape the labor force and reshape practice* in their wake.

Throughout AI's history, the word "imaginary" was rarely used. But the phenomenon was everywhere — in Wiener's proclamations about cybernetics, in Terminator sequels, in tech CEO keynotes, in faculty abstinence policies. This timeline traces those visions, who made them, what they predicted, and what they left behind.

**Adam Prumm's "imaginaries lifecycle"** (from his 2025 literature review) frames how these visions travel:

> Industry imaginaries → shape academic programs → shape student expectations → students carry them into the workforce → workforce expectations feed back into industry leadership

Misalignment accumulates at every transition in this cycle.

---

## Quick Reference Table

| Wave | Era | Dominant Imaginary | Who Proclaimed It | Key Fear |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | 1943–1966 | The Universal Machine — intelligence is information; machines will think | Scientists, military, mathematicians | Machines replacing human cognition at scale |
| **2** | 1966–1987 | The Expert & The Factory — AI encodes expert knowledge; blue-collar work at risk | AI researchers, industrial engineers, corporations | Factory job loss; AI winter disillusionment |
| **3** | 1987–2010 | The Safe Knowledge Worker — cognitive/creative work is automation-proof | Tech industry, economists, management theorists | System optimization, not human replacement |
| **4** | 2010–2019 | The Automation Panic — everything is now at risk, including white-collar work | Frey & Osborne, media, consultancies, Big Tech | Mass unemployment; 47% of jobs automated |
| **5** | 2019–present | Contested Imaginaries — tool, collaborator, or existential threat? | Practitioners, artists, researchers, executives | Creative displacement; who owns the future? |

---

## Wave 1: The Universal Machine (1943–1966)

### The Imaginary
**"Intelligence is information processing. Machines will think — and thinking is a universal, computable process."** *(Prumm, 2025)*

This imaginary was constructed almost entirely by scientists and mathematicians, largely working under military funding during and after WWII. Its core claim: that the brain is a machine, that machines can be brains, and that this equivalence would unlock control over any complex system — organisms, economies, societies.

### Scientific Proclamations
- **Norbert Wiener** — *Cybernetics: Control and Communication in Animal and Machine* (1948): coined "cybernetics" and argued that feedback, information, and control were universal principles governing biological and mechanical systems equally
- **Claude Shannon** — *A Mathematical Theory of Communication* (1948

# AI Imaginaries, Design Education, and the Transformation of Design Practice (Prumm, 2025)

## Summary
This literature review traces how sociotechnical imaginaries about AI have shaped design education and professional design practice across five historical waves (1943–present). Drawing on Jasanoff & Kim's framework of sociotechnical imaginaries, the review synthesizes scholarship from STS, HCI, instructional design, human performance technology, and design studies to argue that misalignment between industry AI imaginaries and academic program responses produces structural gaps in how designers are prepared for AI-integrated practice. The review introduces an "imaginaries lifecycle" model describing how industry visions propagate through academic programs, student expectations, and back into the workforce.

## Key Concepts
- **Sociotechnical imaginaries**: Collectively held visions of AI-enabled futures that shape institutional decisions before the technology matures (Jasanoff & Kim)
- **Imaginaries lifecycle**: The propagation pathway from industry imaginary → academic program → student expectation → workforce → industry feedback
- **Underperforming imaginaries**: AI transformation narratives that reshape labor and practice even when predictions fail to materialize (Stanusch et al., 2024)
- **Design education gap**: The lag between AI capability shifts and curricular adaptation in design programs

## Theoretical Framework
Sociotechnical imaginaries (Jasanoff & Kim); Science and Technology Studies; sociology of professions; instructional design theory; human performance technology.

## Methods
Systematic literature review synthesizing sources across HCI, STS, design studies, AI ethics, labor economics, and instructional technology.

## Main Arguments
1. Each wave of AI development has been accompanied by a distinct imaginary that restructures how design education is justified, organized, and evaluated
2. Design programs have repeatedly lagged behind industry imaginaries, producing graduates misaligned with actual AI-integrated practice
3. The current wave (generative AI) presents a three-way contested imaginary — AI as tool, collaborator, or threat — with no institutional consensus
4. HPT and instructional design frameworks offer systematic approaches to closing the imaginary-practice gap

# AI Impact on Diversity and Job Displacement in ICT (Brown dissertation)

## Summary
Brown's 2025 doctoral dissertation investigates the relationship between AI integration, workforce diversity, and job displacement in the ICT industry using a quantitative correlational study. Surveying 25-question instruments administered to ICT professionals in leadership roles, the study finds statistically significant evidence that AI integration correlates with both reduced workforce diversity and increased job displacement. Grounded in Socio-technical Systems theory and change management frameworks, the study argues for proactive policy and organizational strategies to mitigate bias and support reskilling.

## Key Concepts
- AI and workforce diversity in ICT
- Job displacement (AI-driven automation)
- Socio-technical Systems (STS) theory
- Quantitative correlational research design
- Reskilling and upskilling policy

## Theoretical Framework
Uses Socio-technical Systems theory as the primary lens, emphasizing interdependence of technical and social dimensions in organizational effectiveness; secondary framework from change management (Lewin, Kotter) to analyze organizational adaptation.

## Methods
Quantitative correlational study; online survey instrument (25 questions) administered to ICT industry professionals with leadership experience and AI familiarity; statistical analyses to explore variable relationships and identify disparities.

## Main Arguments
- AI integration in ICT is associated with reduced diversity — compounding pre-existing inequities in a sector already demographically skewed
- Job displacement is a measurable correlate of AI adoption, not merely a future risk; ICT leaders must engage with it as a present challenge
- Organizations that treat AI adoption as purely technical without social and workforce dimensions will amplify inequality while undermining long-term organizational sustainability
- Policy must move beyond principles to workforce assessments, training programs, and accountability mechanisms

## Limitations
- Correlational design cannot establish causality; many confounding variables in ICT labor markets
- Survey sample limited to leadership roles; frontline workers most affected by displacement are underrepresented
- Single sector study; findings may not generalize beyond ICT

## Connections
Relates to [[AI Failure Loops in Devalued Work (Kawakami et al.)]] on occupational devaluation in AI contexts; connects to [[Beyond Design and Use Studying Intelligent Technologies (Bailey and Barley)]] on long-run organizational effects; links to [[Rethinking AI in Organization and Management (Ramaul et al.)]] on AI's organizational implications.

# AI Industry Expectations and Underperforming Imaginaries (Stanusch et al., 2024)

## Summary
Reports a multi-institutional collaborative study of AI industry imaginaries across academia, platform companies, and civil society, arguing that dominant AI narratives function as 'underperforming imaginaries'—visions that reshape institutional practice and resource allocation even when they fail to materialize technically. Drawing on comparative content analysis of industry discourse and expert interviews, the paper maps how expectation cycles are sustained through repeated forecasting, reframing, and institutional investment in unrealized futures.

## Key Concepts

- **Expectation cycles**: Recurring patterns of AI hype, partial delivery, and reframing that sustain imaginary momentum
- **Industry discourse analysis**: Comparative study of how different institutional sectors construct AI futures

## Main Arguments
1. AI industry imaginaries are underperforming in technical terms but overperforming in institutional impact
2. Expectation cycles sustain imaginary momentum even through repeated failures to deliver
3. The gap between imaginary and performance is itself generative—producing new rounds of investment and narrative

1. Design students are aware of AI's potential but lack structured competencies to use it critically and ethically
2. Curricular integration of AI must address both technical skills and ethical reasoning

# AI Literacy and Attitudes Towards AI in Design Education: A

## Summary
This paper investigates design students' AI literacy levels and their attitudes toward AI tools in design education, using survey and assessment instruments to map the relationship between AI understanding and AI adoption willingness. The study finds that students with higher AI literacy report more nuanced attitudes — neither blanket enthusiasm nor rejection — and demonstrate more sophisticated strategies for AI tool evaluation and use. The paper argues that AI literacy education is essential in design programs not just for technical competence but for cultivating the critical attitudes necessary for responsible AI use.

## Key Concepts
- AI literacy framework (awareness, use, evaluation, ethics)
- Student attitudes toward AI in design
- AI literacy assessment in design education
- Critical AI adoption vs. naive adoption
- AI education integration in design curricula

## Theoretical Framework
AI literacy frameworks (Long & Magerko; Touretzky et al.); technology acceptance theory; draws on digital literacy education research to contextualize AI literacy in design education.

## Methods
Survey study with design students; AI literacy assessment instruments; quantitative analysis of relationships between literacy scores and attitude measures; descriptive statistics and correlation analysis.

## Main Arguments
- AI literacy significantly predicts the sophistication of student attitudes toward AI in design — more literate students show more nuanced, critical stances
- Most design students have high AI use interest but low AI evaluation skills, creating a literacy gap that education must address
- AI literacy in design contexts includes design-specific competencies (evaluating AI aesthetics, understanding bias in generated images) beyond general AI literacy frameworks
- Design programs need explicit AI literacy education, not just AI tool integration

## Limitations & Critiques
Self-reported literacy measures may not accurately capture actual capabilities; attitudes toward AI are rapidly shifting as tools evolve; the design student sample may not generalize across design disciplines or geographic contexts.

## Summary
Schauer et al. conduct a comparative study of AI literacy curricula and student competencies across design programs at HTW Berlin, examining how design students at different educational stages understand, use, and critically evaluate AI tools. The study identifies significant variation in AI literacy across programs and student cohorts, with a gap between technical competence and critical/ethical reasoning. The paper proposes curricular recommendations for design programs seeking to develop AI literacy as an integrated professional competency rather than an add-on module.

- Comparative curricular analysis
- Critical AI reasoning vs. technical competence

# AI Rivalry as a Craft: Writing Professionals (Varanasi et al. NYU)

## Summary
Varanasi, Wiesenfeld, and Nov report on how 25 writing professionals navigate generative AI through the lens of Job Crafting theory, identifying four distinct strategies: some resist GAI to maximize human potential and preserve identity, while others embrace it to enhance workflows and take on new AI-managerial labor. The paper shows that GAI adoption is not binary acceptance or rejection but a complex, ongoing process of role reshaping that has identity implications alongside practical workflow effects. It contributes empirical richness to debates about professional futures in the age of GAI.

## Key Concepts
- Job Crafting theory (Wrzesniewski & Dutton)
- GAI resistance and embracing as strategic choices
- Professional identity and credibility preservation
- AI-managerial labor (new work created by managing AI outputs)
- Invisible work amplification through AI

## Theoretical Framework
Job Crafting theory — the idea that workers proactively shape their job boundaries, tasks, and relationships — applied to explain how writing professionals actively restructure their roles in response to GAI pressure rather than passively adapting.

## Methods
25 semi-structured interviews with writing professionals who adopted and/or resisted GAI (screenwriters, paralegals, journalists, marketing writers, etc.); thematic analysis using Job Crafting as interpretive framework.

## Main Arguments
- Writing professionals employ four GAI-response strategies: maximize human potential, reinforce identity, carve niche, preserve credibility (resistance strategies) vs. enhance workflow, minimize mundane tasks, manage AI outputs (adoption strategies)
- GAI resistance is an active, strategic practice, not merely technophobia
- Embracing GAI creates new invisible labor (managing, prompting, verifying AI outputs) that is not yet recognized or compensated
- Professional identity is as much a driver of AI adoption/rejection as practical utility

## Limitations & Critiques
Sample recruited via snowball/purposive sampling and may overrepresent writers who are already reflective about their GAI practices; the study's qualitative nature limits claims about prevalence of each strategy across the broader profession.

# AI-assisted Learning in HCI Education (Heyer et al. Malmo)

## Summary
Heyer, Nilsson, and Pedersen present findings from group interviews and a survey study with interaction design bachelor students at Malmö University examining how motivated learners use and think about GenAI tools in their education. Contrary to dominant institutional narratives emphasizing prohibition and ethical risk, students demonstrate nuanced, self-regulated GenAI use guided by their pride in learning and personal accomplishment. Students are aware of ethical concerns but make considered choices about when and how to use AI — with educators playing a surprisingly limited role in shaping these practices.

## Key Concepts
- Student GenAI use in HCI/interaction design education
- Self-regulated learning and GenAI
- Student identity and pride in accomplishment
- Ethics of AI use in higher education
- Educator role in shaping AI practices

## Theoretical Framework
Grounded in student-centered learning research and identity formation in higher education; challenges institutional framing of GenAI primarily as academic integrity risk; draws on self-determination theory to explain motivation-based AI use.

## Methods
Group interviews (3 groups, 6 students total) and online survey (25 respondents) with interaction design bachelor students spanning first to final year; qualitative thematic analysis of interview data; survey for triangulation.

## Main Arguments
- Students use GenAI in nuanced, context-sensitive ways — their primary regulator is their sense of accomplishment and learning integrity, not institutional policy
- Moralistic and disciplinary institutional rhetoric is largely ineffective because it misunderstands students' actual motivations and practices
- Students navigate a complex terrain of identity questions: what does it mean to learn, to create, to achieve, when AI can assist?
- Educators are largely absent from students' GenAI practice development — a gap that presents both a risk (unguided development) and an opportunity (authentic student agency)

## Limitations
- Small qualitative sample from one Scandinavian institution; findings reflect a specific educational culture
- Focuses on motivated learners — students who struggle or use GenAI problematically may have different patterns

# AI-assisted Learning in HCI Education

## Summary
This paper examines how AI-assisted learning tools are being integrated into HCI education specifically, investigating how AI tutors, code assistants, and feedback systems affect HCI learning outcomes, student engagement, and the development of human-centered design skills. The study finds that AI assistance in HCI courses can support technical skill development effectively but shows mixed results for developing the empathy, contextual reasoning, and critical reflection that are central to HCI practice. The paper calls for HCI-specific AI learning tool design that preserves the discipline's distinctive pedagogical values.

## Key Concepts
- AI-assisted learning in HCI courses
- AI tutoring for technical HCI skills
- Empathy and contextual reasoning in AI-mediated HCI education
- HCI-specific pedagogical values and AI tools
- Learning outcome assessment in AI-assisted HCI courses

## Theoretical Framework
HCI pedagogy; AI in education; constructivist learning; draws on HCI learning science research and AI tutoring literature.

## Methods
Empirical study of AI-assisted learning tools in HCI courses; comparison of learning outcomes with and without AI assistance; student and instructor surveys; qualitative analysis of AI-assisted design work quality.

## Main Arguments
- AI assistance improves technical HCI skill development (prototyping, usability evaluation, coding) but shows limited benefit for developing empathic user research skills
- The efficiency gains from AI assistance in HCI courses may come at the cost of the reflective struggle that builds deeper design reasoning
- HCI educators must be intentional about which course activities benefit from AI support and which must remain unaugmented
- AI learning tools designed for HCI must preserve the discipline's user-centered epistemology, not just optimize for information transfer

## Limitations & Critiques
Single-discipline study may not generalize; learning outcome measures may not capture tacit HCI skill development; the rapid evolution of AI tools makes specific findings time-sensitive.

# AI-Driven Learning Approaches in the Era of Artificial

## Summary
This paper provides a broad overview of AI-driven learning approaches emerging in the current era of advanced AI, examining how machine learning, large language models, and adaptive systems are transforming educational delivery, personalization, and assessment. The paper evaluates the promise and risks of AI-driven learning across formal education, corporate training, and self-directed learning contexts. It argues for learning design principles that harness AI's personalization and feedback capabilities while maintaining the social, motivational, and identity-formation dimensions of learning that AI cannot replicate.

## Key Concepts
- AI-driven learning systems (adaptive learning, LLM tutors)
- Personalized learning at scale
- AI assessment and feedback
- Social and motivational dimensions of learning
- Learning design principles for AI era

## Theoretical Framework
Educational technology; AI in education; learning sciences; draws on adaptive learning research, personalization theory, and learning design frameworks.

## Methods
Conceptual review and synthesis of AI-driven learning research across contexts; evaluation of emerging approaches against learning theory principles; case analysis of deployed AI learning systems.

## Main Arguments
- AI-driven learning offers genuine improvements in personalization, feedback frequency, and learning efficiency for well-defined skills
- The social, motivational, and identity dimensions of learning are not well-served by AI-driven approaches and require human instructor presence
- Learning design for AI-augmented education must explicitly preserve the social and identity-formation dimensions that AI cannot provide
- Equity implications of AI-driven learning are significant: the same tools that personalize learning for some may create new digital divides for others

## Limitations & Critiques
The review spans very heterogeneous AI approaches and educational contexts; evidence quality for many AI-driven learning systems is limited; the field is moving faster than systematic evidence can accumulate.

# Anatomy of Prototypes (Lim Stolterman Tenenberg)

## Summary
Lim, Stolterman, and Tenenberg propose a conceptual framework — an "anatomy of prototypes" — for understanding what prototypes fundamentally are and how they function in design practice. Based on two case studies, they identify two key dimensions: prototypes as filters (they selectively foreground certain design qualities by filtering out others) and prototypes as manifestations (they make design ideas concrete and communicable). This framework reframes prototypes from mere evaluation tools to active generators of design thinking throughout the design process.

## Key Concepts
- Prototypes as filters
- Prototypes as manifestations of design ideas
- Design space exploration
- Fidelity vs. filtering distinction
- Prototype anatomy (what a prototype is, not just what it does)

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on design theory and HCI practice; explicitly moves beyond fidelity-based (low/high) categorizations to a functional/ontological account of what prototyping does in design; informed by Buxton's sketching perspective and design cognition research.

## Methods
Two case studies of design practice in which prototyping was central; grounded analysis to derive the filter/manifestation dimensions; conceptual framework synthesis.

## Main Arguments
- The dominant HCI view of prototypes as evaluation tools captures only a fraction of their actual use — most prototyping is generative and exploratory, not evaluative
- The filtering dimension explains why prototypes work: by strategically ignoring most design qualities, a prototype focuses attention on specific aspects, enabling targeted exploration
- The manifestation dimension explains why prototypes matter: they externalize internal design ideas, making them available for reflection, critique, and communication
- Fidelity alone is a misleading descriptor — two prototypes can have the same fidelity but very different filtering profiles

## Limitations
- Two-case empirical basis; anatomy may not cover all prototype functions across different design domains and modalities
- Framework is descriptive/analytical rather than directly prescriptive about when to use which prototype type

## Connections
Links to [[Designerly Ways of Knowing (Cross 1982)]] on modelling as core design method; relates to [[Educating for Design Character (Boling Gray Smith)]] on design practice; informs [[Metacognitive Support Agents for Human-AI Co-Creation (Gmeiner et al. CMU)]] on AI-mediated design exploration.

# Animo Nullius: AI Origin Story and Data Colonialism (Penn 2023)

## Summary
Penn traces elements of AI's theoretical origins to the social dynamics of capitalism rather than to neurophysiology, arguing that early American AI researchers borrowed from the observation of social phenomena (markets, administration, game theory) to formalize mental behavior mathematically. Penn introduces "animo nullius" — "no person's mind" — as a heuristic naming the rhetorical maneuver by which corporations veil the enclosure of the data commons by appealing to AI's scientific legitimacy. Drawing parallels between historical colonialism's "terra nullius" doctrine and contemporary data practices, Penn argues AI's foundational metaphors naturalize acts of data seizure.

## Key Concepts
- Animo nullius (rhetorical device naturalizing data seizure)
- Data colonialism
- AI's social metaphorical origins (markets, administration, game theory)
- Post-war corporate and military investment in AI
- Assetization of data commons

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on history of science, political economy, and postcolonial theory; relates AI's intellectual genealogy to the dynamics of assetization in modern technoscience; frames data colonialism as a structural parallel (not mere metaphor) to historical colonial dispossession.

## Methods
Historical and conceptual analysis; close reading of founding AI researchers' texts (Minsky, Simon, Rosenblatt, Wiener); archival and secondary source research on post-war corporate/military funding structures; theoretical synthesis.

## Main Arguments
- AI's foundational metaphors (mind-as-computer, society-as-system) were borrowed from social observation, not neural science — importing assumptions about rationality, order, and predictability from capitalist social dynamics
- Post-war corporate and military investment shaped which AI research programs flourished, encoding commercial and imperial logics into the field's assumptions
- Contemporary tech corporations' claim that AI's scientific authority legitimizes their data practices is an "animo nullius" move: declaring the data commons as having no owner to claim it
- Historical colonialism and data colonialism share structural features: dispossession, naturalization through authority claims, and erasure of prior relationships to the commons

## Limitations
- Genealogical argument is selective; AI research traditions are heterogeneous and cannot be fully reduced to capitalist social logic origins
- "Animo nullius" as a concept is evocative but its analytical precision and policy implications need further development

## Connections
Relates to [[Do Artifacts Have Politics (Winner 1980)]] on technology and power; links to [[Co-Producing AI Augmented Participatory Lifecycle (Mushkani et al. UdeM)]] on AI governance and dispossession; connects to [[Rethinking AI in Organization and Management (Ramaul et al.)]] on theorizing AI origins and assumptions.

# Art Education in the Era of Artificial Intelligence (iJET, 2025)

## Summary
This study examines technological anxiety among art practitioners and students triggered by AI-generated content, analyzing anti-AI movements on platforms such as ArtStation and GitHub. It argues that anxiety centers on intellectual property disputes and fears of occupational substitution, and proposes strategies—including emphasizing core artistic values and improving educator AI proficiency—to alleviate that anxiety.

## Key Concepts
- Technological anxiety
- Intellectual property in generative AI
- Occupational substitution
- Compliance anxiety
- Core artistic values

## Theoretical Framework
Dialectical analysis from four perspectives (technology, legal principles, user perspectives, and historical context) is used to interrogate the rationality of anti-AI resistance and to surface underlying structural causes of anxiety.

## Methods
Qualitative; content analysis and case studies tracking social media movements (ArtStation, GitHub), prominent industry figures' remarks, and art school graduation exhibition reviews. No direct artist interviews.

## Main Arguments
- Technological anxiety in the art world is primarily driven by IP and job replacement fears that are partly irrational when examined dialectically
- Anti-AI movements contain legitimate concerns but also overcorrect against tools that could be integrated thoughtfully
- Core artistic values (emotional expression, craftsmanship) are not replaceable by AI and should anchor art education
- Teacher AI proficiency is a key leverage point for reducing student compliance anxiety

## Limitations & Critiques
The study draws on Chinese institutional contexts and publicly visible social media cases rather than direct artist interviews, which limits generalizability; proposed solutions are prescriptive rather than empirically tested.

# Competences for the Modern Designer: Systematic Literature Review (2026)


## Abstract
Higher education institutions offering education in design need to review their teaching content in relation to a changing society and digitalization. In emerging post-digital era higher education is in a state of change. Metacognitive skills and a focus on digitalized world’s competencies are becoming integral components of curricula in modern days. During the 21 st century emphasis in design education has been on design thinking, user-centered design, and the utilization of service designers. On the other hand, contemporary designers are expected to have the capacity to navigate complexity and address wicked problems. Designers are now being called upon to contribute to complex problems, in a highly decentralized and heterogeneous contexts within development processes that are increasingly connected. The change in the field of design and in the professional definition is so rapid that there is no curriculum that can predict the future. This raises two research questions: What are future competences for designers? How these changes should be considered in the design education? The scope of this systematic literature review encompasses scholarly works published in international peer-reviewed academic journals during the period spanning from 1.1.2018 to 31.3.2024. The primary objective is to discern evolving perceptions of the design profession in the future and to identify the key competencies that emerging designers should adeptly master as they navigate the landscape of a digitalized working environment.

**DOI:** [10.1177/14740222251342646](https://doi.org/10.1177/14740222251342646)

## Summary
This 2026 systematic literature review examines the competences required for modern designers, synthesizing recent research to update understanding of design expertise in contexts where AI tools have become pervasive. The review identifies core stable competencies (empathy, systems thinking, conceptual development, iteration) alongside new AI-mediated competencies (AI direction, quality evaluation of AI outputs, ethical AI use). The paper argues that the core of design expertise is shifting from production skills toward meta-cognitive and judgment competencies that complement AI capabilities.

## Key Concepts
- Modern designer competencies framework
- Systematic literature review methodology
- Stable vs. AI-emergent competences in design
- Metacognitive design competences
- Design judgment in AI-mediated practice

## Theoretical Framework
Competency-based education; design expertise research; systematic review methodology; draws on design education and professional competency literature from 2010-2026 to identify shifts in the competency landscape.

## Methods
Systematic literature review following PRISMA protocol; analysis of design competency frameworks from design education, professional organization, and empirical research sources; coding and synthesis of competency categories and their AI-era evolution.

## Main Arguments
- Core design competencies centered on empathy, systems thinking, and conceptual development remain stable and central in the AI era
- New AI-specific competencies (directing AI, evaluating AI quality, ethical AI deployment) are now necessary additions to the design competency framewor

# Using Generative AI Tools in Collaborative UX Design Courses


## Abstract
Artificial Intelligence and their derived Generative technologies are playing a cru - cial role in many applications that involve an active collaboration among machine assistants and human users. That is the case for User Experience courses that al - lowed students and instructors work together with Generative Artificial Intelligence tools to produce a collaborative design. The main purpose of this research consisted in reviewing several stages in design tasks that could take advantage of Artificial Intelligence tools by boosting a prompt-based conversation among instructors and students. Results obtained through the use of these tools demonstrated their huge potential in facilitating co-creative tasks. In this context, a first cohort of students was able to collaborate on the ideation of User Experience projects by exchanging prompts to define persona profiles and checking their suitability. A second cohort was involved in the joint assessment of testing mockups related

**DOI:** [10.1007/s40593-025-00518-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00518-1)

## Summary
This paper examines how design educators integrated generative AI tools into collaborative UX design courses, documenting the pedagogical strategies, student experiences, and learning outcomes that emerged. The study finds that AI tools can enhance collaborative ideation and rapid prototyping while creating new tensions around individual contribution, creative ownership, and skill development. The authors develop recommendations for educators on how to structure AI-assisted collaborative design projects to maximize learning without undermining the collaborative skills that UX education seeks to develop.

## Key Concepts
- Generative AI in UX design education
- Collaborative design with AI tools
- Pedagogical scaffolding for AI-assisted work
- Group creative process and AI mediation
- Assessment in AI-assisted collaborative courses

## Theoretical Framework
Collaborative learning theory; design pedagogy; CSCW perspectives on AI-mediated teamwork; draws on project-based learning frameworks.

## Methods
Qualitative study of multiple UX design courses integrating AI tools; student surveys, focus groups, and design artifact analysis; instructor reflective practice documentation.

## Main Arguments
- AI tools change the division of labor in collaborative design projects in ways that require new pedagogical scaffolding
- Without explicit instruction, students tend to use AI to bypass collaborative negotiation rather than to enhance it
- Effective AI-assisted collaboration requires structured activities that preserve human-to-human creative dialogue
- Assessment must evolve to evaluate the quality of AI direction and curation, not just final design outputs

## Limitations & Critiques
Study conducted during rapid AI tool evolution; findings may not transfer to different course structures or student populations; long-term effects on collaborative design skill development are not tracked.

# Artificial Intelligence as a Tool for Individual and Collaborative Creativity in Design Education


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.1016/j.yjoc.2024.100079](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yjoc.2024.100079)

Integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the design process is a growing area of research interest. Three years after its public launch in 2022, AI has already established itself as the most disruptive tool revolutionizing how designers conceptualize, iterate and innovate. As AI technologies continue to evolve, it is pertinent that design students are acquainted with the potential of the technology and how it can be integrated in their professional practice. The objective of this paper is to explore the role of AI as a conceptualization and research tool in interior design. We aim to examine its effectiveness in enhancing the ideation process and facilitating collaboration and knowledge sharing in intercultural design teams. The case study presented is a collaborative online international learning project (COIL) with the participation of

## Summary
This paper investigates generative AI as a tool for supporting both individual and collaborative creativity in design education, examining how students and faculty use AI during ideation, iteration, and concept development. Through case studies of AI-integrated design courses, the authors find that AI tools open new creative possibilities and lower barriers to visual ideation, but also raise concerns about the homogenization of student work and the erosion of individual creative voice. The paper argues for pedagogical frameworks that cultivate students' capacity to use AI creatively while preserving distinctive design perspectives.

## Key Concepts
- AI as creativity tool (individual and collaborative)
- Design ideation with generative AI
- Creative homogenization risk
- Individual creative voice in AI-mediated design
- Collaborative creativity with AI mediation

## Theoretical Framework
Creativity theory; collaborative cognition; design education pedagogy; draws on componential model of creativity (Amabile) and social creativity frameworks.

## Methods
Multiple case studies of design courses integrating AI for creative tasks; qualitative analysis of student work, reflections, and interviews about AI's role in their creative process.

## Main Arguments
- AI tools significantly lower the barrier to visual ideation, enabling students to generate more concepts faster
- Collaborative creativity benefits from AI when it serves as a shared ideation partner rather than an individual shortcut
- Without pedagogical intervention, AI use tends to converge student outputs toward aesthetically similar results
- Design education must develop students' capacity to use AI creatively — including knowing when not to use it

## Limitations & Critiques
Case study design limits generalizability; the homogenization risk may be tool-specific and evolve as AI models improve; measuring "individual creative voice" empirically remains challenging.

# Automate Infomate: Two Faces of Intelligent Technology (Zuboff 1985)

## Summary
Zuboff's 1985 paper introduces the foundational distinction between automating and informating as two fundamentally different ways intelligent technology transforms work. Automating replaces human labor with machine execution of tasks. Informating — Zuboff's original coinage — occurs when the same systems simultaneously generate information about the processes they automate, creating new possibilities for organizational learning, control, and transformation. Zuboff argues that most organizations choose automating while missing the transformative potential of informating, often because informating threatens existing managerial power structures.

## Key Concepts
- Automating vs. informating
- Intelligent technology (Zuboff's term for computer-mediated work)
- Textualization of work (information rendering)
- Panopticon dynamics and electronic surveillance
- Organizational learning and knowledge transparency

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on phenomenology of work, labor process theory, and organizational sociology; influenced by Foucault (panopticon), Habermas (communicative action), and Marx (labor transformation); grounded in ethnographic field research.

## Methods
Multi-site qualitative study of manufacturing plants, offices, and financial services organizations undergoing computerization in the early 1980s; ethnographic observation and in-depth interviews.

## Main Arguments
- Every intelligent technology simultaneously automates and informates — but organizations must choose whether to exploit the informating potential or suppress it
- Informating creates a "data-presence" of work that renders previously tacit processes transparent and subject to new kinds of analysis
- This transparency is politically charged: it can enable worker learning and empowerment OR managerial surveillance and deskilling, depending on organizational choices
- The choice to informate requires fundamentally rethinking managerial authority, since information access threatens hierarchical control

## Limitations
- Empirical context is early computer-mediated manufacturing/office work; contemporary AI systems have informating dynamics of much greater scope and speed
- Normative vision (informating as democratizing potential) reflects 1980s techno-optimism; surveillance dynamics have proven more dominant in practice

## Connections
Foundational for [[Beyond Design and Use Studying Intelligent Technologies (Bailey and Barley)]] and [[AI Failure Loops in Devalued Work (Kawakami et al.)]]; relates to [[Do Artifacts Have Politics (Winner 1980)]] on technology and power; connects to [[Rethinking AI in Organization and Management (Ramaul et al.)]] on AI theorization.
