## Summary
This practitioner-oriented paper examines methods and frameworks for integrating AI into the design process across multiple design disciplines, offering a taxonomy of AI integration points and design process stages where AI adds most value. Drawing on case studies from product design, graphic design, and UX, the paper argues that AI integration is most effective when designed around the designer's process rather than around the AI tool's capabilities. The paper provides practical frameworks for designers seeking to systematically incorporate AI into professional practice.

## Key Concepts
- AI integration in design process
- Design process stage analysis (research, ideation, prototyping, production)
- AI as process augmentation vs. replacement
- Human oversight in AI-integrated design
- Taxonomy of AI design tools by function

## Theoretical Framework
Design process methodology; human-centered AI integration; draws on established design process models (double diamond, UCD) to organize AI integration strategy.

## Methods
Multiple case studies across design disciplines; practitioner documentation and reflection; taxonomy development from empirical cases; literature review of AI design tool capabilities.

## Main Arguments
- AI integration works best when it augments specific, bounded phases of the design process rather than being applied uniformly across all design work
- Designers who understand their own process can identify the highest-value AI integration points; those who don't tend toward superficial AI use
- Human oversight and editorial judgment remain essential at all stages of AI-integrated design work
- The taxonomy of AI tools by design function helps designers match tools to process needs rather than adopting tools opportunistically

## Limitations & Critiques
Case study evidence is primarily from design disciplines with strong visual output; service design and systems design integration is less thoroughly addressed; the pace of AI tool development means specific tool recommendations will date quickly.

# Integrating AI in Literacy Lessons for Elementary Classrooms: A Co-Design Approach

## Summary
This paper presents a co-design study for integrating AI into literacy lessons in elementary classrooms, documenting a collaborative process in which teachers, designers, and researchers co-created AI-integrated literacy activities for early elementary students. The study examines how co-design methodology surfaces teacher pedagogical concerns, student developmental considerations, and institutional constraints that would be missed in top-down AI curriculum development. The paper contributes both a co-designed curriculum artifact and a co-design methodology for AI-integrated elementary education.

## Key Concepts
- Co-design for AI-integrated literacy education
- Elementary literacy and AI tools
- Teacher-researcher-designer collaboration
- Co-design methodology for curriculum development
- AI in early literacy contexts

## Theoretical Framework
Co-design and participatory design; literacy education; constructivist curriculum design; draws on co-design methodology (Sanders & Stappers) and early literacy pedagogy.

## Methods
Participatory co-design study; iterative design workshops with teachers, researchers, and designers; implementation and qualitative evaluation of co-designed AI literacy activities; thematic analysis of co-design process and outcomes.

## Main Arguments
- Co-design is essential for AI curriculum development in elementary contexts because teachers have pedagogical knowledge that AI and technology experts lack
- Co-designed AI literacy activities better fit classroom constraints and developmental appropriateness than expert-designed equivalents
- The co-design process itself generates teacher buy-in and professional learning that supports effective implementation
- AI integration in early literacy requires particular sensitivity to developmental stage and must complement rather than replace foundational literacy instruction

## Limitations & Critiques
Single school/district co-design context; co-design processes are resource-intensive and may not scale; the specific AI tools integrated will evolve quickly; long-term literacy outcome data from AI-integrated approaches is not yet available.

## Summary
Examines how AI practitioners integrate futures imaginaries, expectations, and anticipatory practices into their everyday work, drawing on interviews with Finnish AI developers and researchers. ## Key Concepts
- **Anticipatory practices**: The routinized activities through which practitioners orient their work toward imagined futures
- **Expectations**: Specific, near-term predictions about AI capability that guide resource allocation and project scope
- **Futures imaginaries**: Broader, values-laden visions of what AI could mean for society and work

## Main Arguments
1. Practitioners hold distinct but interrelated futures imaginaries, expectations, and anticipatory practices simultaneously
2. The gap between expectation and imaginary is where most AI project failures and pivots occur
3. Anticipatory practices deserve empirical study as a primary site of AI future-making

# Integrating Unplugged and Plugged for Holistic AI Education (Dai)

## Summary
Dai proposes an "embodied constructionist approach" to AI education that integrates unplugged activities (physical analogies, embodied simulation) with plugged activities (direct interaction with AI systems) to achieve holistic AI literacy. Using design-based research (DBR) over two years with 107 sixth graders, the study implements and refines a cyclical understand–make–reflect process. Students progressively comprehend conceptual, technical, and ethical dimensions of AI through this embodied constructionist framework, outperforming approaches that treat these dimensions separately.

## Key Concepts
- Embodied constructionism (hybrid of embodied cognition + Papert's constructionism)
- Unplugged-plugged integration
- Holistic AI literacy (conceptual + technical + ethical)
- Design-based research (DBR)
- Understand–make–reflect cycle

## Theoretical Framework
Synthesizes embodied cognition theory (Lakoff and Johnson), constructionism (Papert), and AI literacy frameworks (Long and Magerko); argues that physical enactment of AI concepts provides cognitive scaffolding for understanding abstract computational processes.

## Methods
Design-based research over two years; authentic classroom implementation with 107 sixth graders; classroom observation, video-recording, student interviews and artifacts, teacher debriefings; case study analysis of learning trajectories.

## Main Arguments
- Abstract AI concepts require embodied analogies before students can engage meaningfully with plugged AI systems — the unplugged → plugged sequence is pedagogically essential, not merely supplementary
- Holistic AI literacy cannot be achieved by compartmentalizing technical, conceptual, and ethical learning — the embodied constructionist approach integrates all three through making and reflecting
- The understand–make–reflect cycle produces more durable and transferable understanding than linear instruction
- Upper primary school is a critical but under-examined developmental window for AI literacy — age-appropriate pedagogy is distinctively needed

## Limitations
- Two-year DBR study in a single school context; generalizability across curricula, teacher profiles, and cultural contexts requires further investigation
- Embodied constructionist approach demands significant teacher preparation and curriculum redesign
- No comparative group; learning gains are assessed through within-group longitudinal analysis

## Connections
Directly links to [[Epistemic Insights AI Ethics via Constructionism (Lin and Dai CUHK)]] (same research group, complementary approach); relates to [[Behaviorism Cognitivism Constructivism Compared (Ertmer and Newby)]] on constructivist theory; connects to [[AI Literacy in Design Education Comparative Study (Schauer et al. HTW Berlin)]] on AI literacy pedagogy.

# Integrating User Experience in User Interface

## Summary
This paper examines the integration of user experience (UX) principles and methods into user interface (UI) design workflows, addressing the persistent gap between UX research and UI production in both professional practice and education. The authors argue that UX and UI are often treated as sequential phases (UX research → UI design) when they are most effective as concurrent, iterative activities. The paper proposes integration frameworks and documents case studies where UX-UI integration produced measurably better outcomes than traditional handoff-based workflows.

## Key Concepts
- UX-UI integration (vs. sequential handoff)
- User research informing UI decisions
- Iterative UX-UI workflow
- Design handoff and collaboration challenges
- UI design education and UX grounding

## Theoretical Framework
User-centered design; iterative design methodology; design collaboration theory; draws on software engineering agile methods and UX practice literature.

## Methods
Case study analysis of UX-UI integrated design projects; comparative analysis with traditional handoff workflows; qualitative data from practitioner interviews about integration challenges and benefits.

## Main Arguments
- The handoff model (UX hands off to UI) produces friction, information loss, and ultimately worse products than integrated workflows
- Effective UX-UI integration requires shared vocabulary, tools, and a culture of continuous user validation throughout UI development
- Design education that separates UX and UI tracks produces practitioners unprepared for the integrated reality of professional practice
- Tools that support shared UX-UI artifacts (annotated prototypes, living design systems) are essential infrastructure for integration

## Limitations & Critiques
Case study design limits generalizability; the integration model requires organizational investment in tools and processes; small teams and freelancers may find the model less applicable than enterprise contexts.

# Exploring the Impact of AI Language Model ChatGPT on User Experience (IJTIM)


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.54489/ijtim.v3i1.195](https://doi.org/10.54489/ijtim.v3i1.195)

This study investigates the integration of AI language model tools, specifically ChatGPT, in the Design Thinking process to evaluate their effect on product design. While previous research has primarily focused on Design Thinking, limited research has been conducted on the application of AI tools in the process. This study involved redesigning two previous projects using AI tools in the Design Thinking process. We conducted interviews with five designers and analysed ten Product Manager reports to understand the impact of using AI tools on one of the most popular innovation and problem-solving approaches called Design Thinking. The findings indicate that integrating AI tools into the design thinking process, specifically in the Define and Ideate stages, can improve the efficiency and creativity of the UI. However, the successful implementation of AI tools requires a combination of technological expertise and creative design thinking. The study emphasizes the potential for AI tools to complement human creativity and expertise in the design process, rather than replace them. The results contribute to understanding the appropriate application of AI tools in design and innovation while underscoring the importance of keeping humans at the centre of the process.

## Summary
This paper examines the impact of ChatGPT on user experience design work, investigating how UX practitioners are incorporating the large language model into research, writing, and prototyping tasks. Through a survey and interview study with UX practitioners, the authors document how ChatGPT is being used to generate interview questions, synthesize research notes, draft UX writing, and explain design rationale — while identifying the accuracy, hallucination, and generic output problems practitioners encounter. The paper provides a practical assessment of ChatGPT's current utility and limitations for UX work.

## Key Concepts
- ChatGPT in UX research and design workflows
- AI hallucination and accuracy concerns in UX
- UX writing and AI text generation
- AI for design documentation and rationale
- Practitioner AI adoption in UX

## Theoretical Framework
Technology assessment; human-AI collaboration in professional practice; UX practice research; draws on technology adoption and practitioner-AI collaboration literature.

## Methods
Mixed-methods study; online survey with UX practitioners; follow-up qualitative interviews; analysis of ChatGPT use patterns, perceived utility, and experienced limitations.

## Main Arguments
- UX practitioners are adopting ChatGPT rapidly for text-heavy tasks (documentation, question generation, synthesizing notes) where it provides genuine time savings
- Hallucination and generic output are the most significant practical concerns, requiring practitioners to develop verification habits

# Points of Contact: Where Learning Sciences and Educational Technology Meet


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.1108/ils-06-2018-0045](https://doi.org/10.1108/ils-06-2018-0045)

Purpose The explosive growth in the number of digital tools utilized in everyday learning activities generates data at an unprecedented scale, providing exciting challenges that cross scholarly communities. This paper aims to provide an overview of learning analytics (LA) with the aim of helping members of the information and learning sciences communities understand how educational Big Data is relevant to their research agendas and how they can contribute to this growing new field. Design/methodology/approach Highlighting shared values and issues illustrates why LA is the perfect meeting ground for information and the learning sciences, and suggests how by working together effective LA tools can be designed to innovate education. Findings Analytics-driven performance dashboards are offered as a specific example of one research area where information and learning scientists can make a significant contribution to LA research. Recent reviews of existing dashboard studies point to a dearth of evaluation with regard to either theory or outcomes. Here, the relevant expertise from researchers in both the learning sciences and information science is offered as an important opportunity to improve the design and evaluation of student-facing dashboards. Originality/value This paper outlines important ties between three scholarly communities to illustrate how their combined research expertise is crucial to advancing how we understand learning and for developing LA-based interventions that meet the values that we all share.

This introductory chapter to a learning sciences handbook section examines the points of contact and productive tensions between the learning sciences and educational technology, two fields that share subject matter but have developed distinct disciplinary identities, methods, and values. # "It's Like the Value System in the Loop": Domain Experts' Values Expectations for NLP Automation (Showkat & Baumer)

## Summary
Showkat and Baumer's paper investigates how domain experts in high-stakes fields (law, medicine, social work) express and negotiate their values expectations for NLP automation tools being designed for their professional contexts. Through interviews and participatory design sessions, the study documents how experts articulate values like accuracy, fairness, explainability, and human oversight — and how these values conflict with each other and with NLP system constraints. The paper contributes frameworks for values negotiation in NLP design and argues for more robust mechanisms for expert values participation in AI system development.

## Key Concepts
- Domain expert values expectations for NLP
- Values negotiation in AI design
- Human oversight and explainability in professional AI
- Accuracy vs. fairness tensions in NLP systems
- Participatory values-sensitive design for AI

## Theoretical Framework
Value Sensitive Design (VSD); participatory design; critical AI studies; draws on Friedman and Hendry's VSD framework and Baumer's prior work on resistance and non-use to examine values in professional NLP contexts.

## Methods
Participatory design sessions and interviews with domain experts (legal, medical, social work) about NLP tools designed for their fields; qualitative analysis of values expressions, tensions, and negotiation strategies.

## Main Arguments
- Domain experts hold complex, context-specific values expectations for NLP automation that generic AI ethics principles do not capture
- Values tensions (accuracy vs. fairness, efficiency vs. human oversight) are not resolvable through design alone — they require ongoing negotiation
- Expert participation in NLP design reveals hidden values that become visible only when experts encounter specific system behaviors
- "The value system in the loop" — keeping values-aware human judgment integrated with automated systems — is an expert demand that current NLP systems fail to fully support

## Limitations & Critiques
Study limited to three professional domains; the participatory design setting may elicit different values expressions than naturalistic AI deployment; NLP capabilities have advanced since the study, potentially changing the values landscape.

# Shaping Human Capital Standards: Exploring the Intersections of the Future of Work and AI (2025)


## Abstract
This study represents a foundational phase in a broader research program designed to guide investors and policymakers in the development of human capital standards. By examining the critical intersections between the future of work and artificial intelligence (AI), it investigates how technological advancements are reshaping workforce dynamics, redefining skill requirements, and influencing human capital strategies. In this initial stage, the study focuses on key issues, including the assessment of risks, opportunities, and uncertainties associated with the integration of AI into workplace practices. Our objective is to develop a comprehensive mapping of human capital components, establishing a solid foundation for evidence-based decision-making. Ultimately, this framework aims to support the creation of robust human capital standards that align with the priorities of investors and policymakers, while promoting transparency, encouraging innovation, and enabling the sustainable creation of long-term value.

**DOI:** [10.61737/NNSO3210](https://doi.org/10.61737/NNSO3210)

## Summary

# Januszewski and Molenda - Educational Technology Definition (2008)

## Summary
Januszewski and Molenda (2008) present the AECT Definition and Terminology Committee's revised definition of educational technology: "the study and ethical practice of facilitating learning and improving performance by creating, using, and managing appropriate technological processes and resources." This foundational chapter elaborates each element of the definition, positioning the field as both a theoretical study and an ethical practice. The revision explicitly adds "ethical practice" to prior definitions and emphasizes performance alongside learning as legitimate field outcomes.

## Key Concepts
- **Educational technology**: Study and ethical practice of facilitating learning and improving performance
- **Study**: Includes research and reflective practice; knowledge construction through inquiry
- **Ethical practice**: Professional responsibility to learners, institutions, and society embedded in the definition
- **Creating, using, managing**: Three functional domains encompassing the field's activities
- **Technological processes and resources**: Both systematic procedures and tools/materials

## Theoretical Framework
Definitional and conceptual work synthesizing prior AECT definitions and responding to field evolution. Reflects the committee's consensus position on how to bound and characterize educational technology as a distinct field.

## Methods
Committee deliberation and literature synthesis, presented as authoritative definition from AECT's official definitional body.

## Main Arguments
1. Educational technology is defined by its purposes (facilitating learning, improving performance) rather than its tools
2. Ethical practice is not optional or external—it is constitutive of what educational technologists do
3. The field's scope encompasses creating new technologies, facilitating their use, and managing their deployment
4. Performance as an explicit goal distinguishes the 2008 definition from prior versions focused solely on learning

## Limitations
Definitional work is inherently contested and reflects the commitments of its authors and the AECT community. Critiqued by Lowenthal & Wilson (2010) for insufficient rationale and practitioner consultation.

# John Zimmerman, Carnegie Mellon University

## Summary
Zimmerman's CMU paper examines how UX designers are advocating for and driving AI integration within enterprise organizations, arguing that UX designers occupy a unique position to bridge technical AI capabilities and human-centered organizational needs. Drawing on case studies of enterprise AI deployments, the paper documents how UX designers are expanding their roles to include AI strategy, prompt engineering, and AI governance — while also identifying the challenges when UX perspectives are marginalized in technical AI development processes. It calls for UX practitioners to claim greater agency in enterprise AI design.

## Key Concepts
- UX designers as AI advocates in enterprise contexts
- Adaptive UIs and AI-driven interface personalization
- Enterprise AI deployment challenges
- UX role expansion in AI organizations
- Human-centered AI governance

## Theoretical Framework
UX practice theory; organizational change and technology adoption; human-centered design in enterprise contexts; draws on Zimmerman's prior work on research through design and the role of design in technology organizations.

## Methods
Case study research; interviews with UX designers and stakeholders in enterprise AI deployment projects; analysis of UX involvement in AI development processes across multiple organizations.

## Main Arguments
- UX designers are de facto AI advocates in enterprise organizations because they translate between AI capabilities and human needs
- Enterprise AI deployments that marginalize UX input produce systems that are technically functional but socially and experientially inadequate
- UX practitioners need expanded competencies (AI literacy, data literacy, governance frameworks) to fulfill their expanding role
- Organizations benefit when UX designers are involved early in AI strategy, not just in interface delivery

## Limitations & Critiques
Enterprise context may not generalize to startups, agencies, or public sector contexts; the case studies reflect a specific moment in enterprise AI adoption; UX practitioners' capacity to influence AI strategy depends heavily on organizational power dynamics.

## Abstract

## Summary
This systematic review examines the emerging literature on human-centric AI in Industry 5.0, analyzing how the Industry 5.0 framework's emphasis on human wellbeing, sustainability, and resilience differs from Industry 4.0's productivity-centered focus. The review synthesizes research on collaborative robots, AI workplace integration, and human-machine collaboration to assess how Industry 5.0 principles are being operationalized. The paper argues that human-centric AI requires not just technical design choices but organizational and policy commitments to worker agency and wellbeing.

- Industry 5.0 (human-centric, sustainable, resilient)
- Industry 4.0 vs. 5.0 comparison
- Human-robot collaboration in manufacturing
- Worker wellbeing and AI design

## Theoretical Framework
Industry 5.0 framework (European Commission); human-centered design; sociotechnical systems theory; draws on manufacturing and workplace AI research.

## Methods
Systematic literature review of Industry 5.0 and human-centric AI research; thematic coding across 60+ studies; analysis of human-centric AI implementation examples and outcomes.

## Main Arguments
- Industry 5.0's human-centric framing represents a genuine paradigm shift from the efficiency-optimization focus of Industry 4.0
- Human-centric AI in manufacturing requires co-design with workers, not just ergonomic design of human-robot interfaces
- Sustainable and resilient AI systems require diversity of approaches and human adaptability, not just technical redundancy
- The transition to Industry 5.0 requires policy interventions and organizational commitments beyond technical capability development

## Limitations & Critiques
Industry 5.0 as a framework is relatively new and some cited implementations may be primarily rhetorical; the review spans heterogeneous manufacturing contexts; the human-centric claims of many Industry 5.0 implementations have not been independently validated.

# From Disruptions to Discussions: How GenAI Impacts Human Interactions in Software Development


## Abstract
*Abstract not yet found — search by title or check source PDF*

**DOI:** [10.1109/tse.2026.3655626](https://doi.org/10.1109/tse.2026.3655626)

## Summary
This paper investigates how generative AI is disrupting and reshaping human interactions in software development teams, examining how AI coding assistants affect collaboration patterns, communication, and team knowledge distribution. Through a study of software development teams using AI code generation tools, the authors find that AI shifts developers' attention from production to review and integration, changes the social dynamics of pair programming and code review, and creates new coordination challenges around AI-generated code ownership and quality. The paper frames these as discussions that teams and organizations must engage proactively.

## Key Concepts
- Generative AI in software development teams
- AI coding assistant effects on collaboration
- Code review and quality assurance in AI-mediated development
- Knowledge distribution in AI-augmented teams
- Human interaction disruption in software development

## Theoretical Framework
CSCW; software engineering practices; human-AI teaming; draws on pair programming research, code review literature, and distributed cognition to analyze AI's effects on development team dynamics.

## Methods
Study of software development teams using AI coding assistants; qualitative interviews and surveys; analysis of development workflow changes; observation of code review and collaboration sessions.

## Main Arguments
- AI coding assistants shift the cognitive work of software development from generation to evaluation, requiring new review competencies
- Pair programming dynamics change when AI is the "partner": the social and epistemic functions of human pair programming are not replicated
- Team knowledge distribution shifts: AI knowledge is external to the team and opaque, creating new dependencies and single points of failure
- Organizations need deliberate policies about AI code use to prevent the erosion of collective code understanding

## Limitations & Critiques
Study conducted at a specific moment in AI coding tool adoption; rapidly improving capabilities may shift findings; team size and organizational context significantly affect findings; the software development context may not generalize to other collaborative work contexts.

# Kirkpatrick Plus: Evaluation and Continuous

## Summary
Watkins, Leigh, Foshay, and Kaufman (2003) propose "Kirkpatrick Plus," an extension of Kirkpatrick's four-level framework adding a fifth level focused on community and societal outcomes. The article argues that contemporary organizations must account for impacts beyond organizational results (Level 4) to include client/customer outcomes and broader social value. Drawing on Kaufman's Organizational Elements Model, the authors integrate Kirkpatrick's internal focus with a systemic, external-facing conception of training's value and responsibility.

## Key Concepts
- **Level 5 (Community outcomes)**: Societal and client/customer impact beyond the organization's own results
- **Kaufman's Organizational Elements Model**: Framework distinguishing inputs, processes, products, outputs, and outcomes at organizational and societal levels
- **Value-added training**: Training that demonstrates contribution to stakeholder value at multiple levels
- **Continuous improvement**: Using evaluation data cyclically to refine training interventions
- **External validity**: Training's responsiveness to needs that extend beyond the employing organization

## Theoretical Framework
Systems theory applied to training evaluation; Kaufman's Mega, Macro, and Micro planning model frames organizational activity in relation to societal outcomes. Extends Kirkpatrick's instrumental framework with a normative dimension.

## Methods
Conceptual integration of Kirkpatrick's framework with Kaufman's organizational elements model. Illustrative case examples and practitioner tools provided.

## Main Arguments
1. Kirkpatrick's four levels are necessary but insufficient; organizations that only evaluate internally miss impacts on clients and society
2. A fifth level (community/societal outcomes) makes training evaluation more responsive to stakeholder accountability demands
3. Continuous improvement requires closing the feedback loop between evaluation findings and training design
4. Training professionals who only demonstrate Level 1–2 results are vulnerable to being dismissed as a cost center

## Limitations
Level 5 evaluation is even more difficult to attribute to training than Level 4; the causal chain becomes highly attenuated. The framework remains primarily prescriptive without strong empirical evidence that adopters produce better training outcomes.

- Directly extends [[EVALUATING]] (Kirkpatrick Four Levels)
- Relates to [[Program Evaluation]] and [[A Comparative Analysis]] on evaluation frameworks
- Connects to [[Stolovitch Beresford 2012--evoluation of HPT (1)]] on performance improvement systemic thinking

# Labels DO Matter (Lowenthal and Wilson)

## Summary
Lowenthal and Wilson (2010, *TechTrends*) critique AECT's 2008 decision to revert from "instructional technology" to "educational technology" as the field's official label, arguing the change was poorly reasoned and practically damaging. Drawing on job posting analysis, program title surveys, and listserv discussions, they demonstrate that "educational technology" is less recognizable and less marketable to corporate and higher education employers than alternatives like "instructional design," "instructional technology," or "learning and development." The authors argue that definitional and labeling choices have real professional consequences that the AECT committee inadequately considered.

## Key Concepts
- **Field labeling**: The choice of what to call a field shapes how it is recognized, hired for, and positioned relative to adjacent fields
- **Professional branding**: Labels function as brand identifiers in job markets
- **AECT 2008 definition**: The committee's reversion to "educational technology" from prior terminology
- **Practitioner vs. academic perspectives**: The 2008 definition may reflect academic commitments that diverge from practitioner needs
- **Market recognition**: Employer familiarity with a field's label affects hiring and program enrollment

## Theoretical Framework
Sociology of professions and professional identity; labels are understood as performative—they shape the field they purport to describe. Empirical evidence from job market analysis grounds the argument in observable professional consequences.

## Methods
Analysis of job postings and program titles; review of AECT listserv discussions; comparative survey of how different terms are used in practitioner and academic contexts.

## Main Arguments
1. The rationale offered by AECT for reverting to "educational technology" was weak and insufficiently attentive to practitioner consequences
2. "Educational technology" is more recognizable in K-12 and higher education settings but less so in corporate training and business contexts
3. The field's multiple competing labels reflect real tensions between academic and practitioner communities
4. Future definitional changes should be made with stronger empirical evidence and broader stakeholder consultation

## Limitations
The job market analysis may not reflect current naming practices; professional labels shift over time and 2010 findings may be outdated. The authors' preference for "instructional technology/design" language reflects their own professional positioning.

## Connections
- Directly critiques [[AECT Definition and Terminology (2008)]] and [[Januszewski and Molenda - Educational Technology Definition (2008)]]
- Relates to [[Reiser (2018)--Chapter 1 What field]] on field identity debates
- Connects to [[Spector 2008 - Theoretical Foundations Ed Communication and Tech]] on the field's theoretical foundations

# Learning from AI’s Previous Awakenings: The History of Expert Systems (Brock, 2018)


## Summary

\
## Summary
Presents an institutional and technical history of expert systems as a "previous awakening" of AI—one of several cycles of intense interest and commercialization followed by disappointment—arguing that today's AI developers should study this history to avoid repeating its failures. Centers on the "knowledge acquisition bottleneck," hype outpacing capability, and misaligned commercialization incentives as structural causes of the first AI winter.

## Key Concepts
- Expert systems and AI winter
- Knowledge acquisition bottleneck
- AI hype cycle
- Commercialization of AI research
- Institutional history of technology

## Theoretical Framework
History of technology with an institutional focus; AI development cycles as recurring patterns of enthusiasm, investment, and disillusionment; lessons-from-history framing for contemporary AI practitioners.

## Methods
Historical analysis drawing on oral histories, archival research, and the May 2018 Computer History Museum pioneer meeting; analysis of technical failures and business dynamics in the expert systems era.

## Main Arguments
- Expert systems succeeded technically in narrow domains but failed commercially due to the knowledge acquisition bottleneck—the enormous labor required to capture and maintain expert knowledge
- Unrealistic expectations set by researchers and vendors created a hype cycle that crashed when expert systems could not scale
- Today's AI developers face structurally similar risks from unchecked hype, narrow benchmarks, and misaligned incentives
- Deep study of the expert systems history offers practical lessons for responsible AI development and deployment

## Limitations & Critiques
Historical perspective may not map cleanly onto deep learning, which learns from data rather than hand-coded rules; the expert systems case is specific in ways that limit direct analogy; the "lessons" are prescriptive and their application to current AI is not straightforward.

# Learning from Notes: Groupware Implementation (Orlikowski 2002)

## Summary
Orlikowski's foundational 1992/2002 paper reports a field study of Lotus Notes groupware implementation at a large professional services firm (Alpha Corporation), finding that the technology failed to achieve its collaborative promise not due to technical limitations but due to mental models and organizational structure. Workers interpreted Notes through the frame of familiar personal productivity software rather than as a collaborative platform; simultaneously, the organization's competitive, individualistic culture provided no incentives for the shared effort and expertise disclosure that Notes required.

## Key Concepts
- Groupware implementation failure
- Technological frames (mental models of technology)
- Organizational culture and structure
- Collaboration-enabling conditions
- Unintended consequences of technology implementation

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on social constructivism and early sociotechnical systems theory; introduces "technological frames" as the interpretive schemas through which organizational members make sense of new technologies; anticipates later structuration-based technology research.

## Methods
Exploratory field study; participant observation and interviews at Alpha Corporation over several months of Notes implementation; qualitative analysis of adoption patterns and social dynamics.

## Main Arguments
- Technology cannot engender collaborative behaviors in organizations where culture and structure work against collaboration — the technology is insufficient by itself
- Mental models (technological frames) shape how technology is interpreted and used: workers framed Notes as a personal tool, not a shared one
- Organizational structure (competitive culture, individual performance incentives) actively discouraged the information sharing Notes was designed to support
- Technology implementation must attend to cognitive and organizational preconditions for the technology's intended use model

## Limitations
- Single organization case study from the early 1990s; enterprise software and organizational norms have changed significantly
- Study focused on initial implementation period; longer-term adoption dynamics may differ

## Connections
Relates to [[Activity Theory for Workplace Learning Technologies (Martinez Marroquin and Senadji)]] on technology-organization fit; links to [[Beyond Design and Use Studying Intelligent Technologies (Bailey and Barley)]] on technology in organizational contexts; connects to [[Automate Infomate Two Faces of Intelligent Technology (Zuboff 1985)]] on technology and organizational transformation.

## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.1016/b978-0-7506-9849-8.50014-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-7506-9849-8.50014-9)

This paper explores the introduction of groupware into an organization to understand the changes in work practices and social interaction facilitated by the technology. The results suggest that people’s mental models and organizations’ structure and culture significantly influence how groupware is implemented and used. Further, the culture and structure provided few incentives or norms for cooperating or sharing expertise, hence the groupware on its own was unlikely to engender collaboration. ## Summary
Orlikowski's 2002 paper documents an organizational case study of Lotus Notes implementation, arguing that the gap between a technology's designed affordances and its actual organizational use reveals how technology adoption is shaped by social structures, power dynamics, and organizational culture rather than technical features alone. The paper develops the concept of "technologies-in-practice" — the enacted technologies that emerge from actual use rather than designed systems — and demonstrates how different groups in the same organization develop radically different practices with the same tool. It is a foundational text for sociomaterial and practice-based approaches to technology in organizations.

## Key Concepts
- Technologies-in-practice (enacted vs. designed technologies)
- Organizational implementation of groupware
- Sociomaterial analysis of technology use
- Unanticipated technology adoption patterns
- Structural dimensions of technology use

## Theoretical Framework
Practice theory (Giddens' structuration theory, extended to technology); sociomaterial approaches; draws on Orlikowski's earlier work on the duality of technology to develop the technologies-in-practice concept.

## Methods
Longitudinal case study of Lotus Notes implementation in a large professional services firm; qualitative data from interviews, observation, and document analysis over multiple years.

## Main Arguments
- Technology's effects in organizations are not determined by its technical features but by the social structures and practices through which it is enacted
- Different organizational groups develop different "technologies-in-practice" with the same tool, reflecting their different structural contexts

- Implementation failures often stem from misalignment between technology assumptions and organizational structure, not from technical inadequacy

# LLM Role in UI UX Design: Systematic Literature Review (Ahmed and Imran)

## Summary
Ahmed and Imran conduct a systematic literature review of empirical and applied research examining the role of large language models (LLMs) in UI/UX design processes. Synthesizing studies across wireframing, user research, accessibility evaluation, design critique, and handoff documentation, the review identifies where LLMs currently add measurable value, where they introduce new risks, and where the gap between LLM capability and professional UX practice requirements is most significant. The paper serves as an evidence base for practitioners and researchers considering LLM integration in UX workflows.

## Key Concepts
- LLMs in UI/UX design workflows
- Systematic literature review methodology
- Wireframing and prototyping with LLMs
- AI-assisted user research
- Accessibility and inclusive design with AI

## Theoretical Framework
Systematic review using PRISMA guidelines; organizes findings by UX design phase (discovery, definition, ideation, prototyping, testing, handoff); evaluates each phase for evidence of LLM contribution and identified limitations.

## Methods
Systematic literature review; database searches (ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, Scopus); screening by title, abstract, and full text; quality appraisal and thematic synthesis across included studies.

## Main Arguments
- LLMs demonstrate consistent value in text-heavy UX tasks: writing user stories, generating interview questions, synthesizing research findings, and drafting design documentation
- For visual and spatial design tasks (wireframing, layout), LLM value is more constrained — they require structured prompting and human refinement to produce usable outputs
- Accessibility evaluation shows promise but LLMs' understanding of disability contexts and edge cases remains inconsistent
- The review reveals a significant gap between academic proof-of-concept studies and evidence from professional practice settings — more ecologically valid research is needed

## Limitations
- Rapidly evolving field; studies included may be superseded by newer model capabilities
- Definitional inconsistency across included studies in what counts as "LLM use" in UX complicates synthesis

# Making the Right Thing: HCI and Responsible AI (Jung et al. CMU)

## Summary
Jung et al. investigate how early-stage AI concept selection — the moment when practitioners choose which AI ideas to pursue — can embed Responsible AI (RAI) principles before substantial investment is made, using a Research through Design approach with three design experiments including a probe study with industry practitioners. They find that multidisciplinary collaboration and structured risk-benefit evaluation tools help practitioners effectively identify low-risk, high-benefit AI concepts. The paper argues for design-led approaches to RAI that engage ethical thinking at the front end of innovation.

## Key Concepts
- Early-stage AI concept selection
- Responsible AI (RAI) principles
- Research through Design
- Multidisciplinary risk-benefit evaluation
- Front-end innovation ethics

## Theoretical Framework
Research through Design (RtD) as the methodological/epistemological framework; synthesizes HCI design methods with RAI scholarship to propose that design practice can operationalize ethical AI principles before systems are built.

## Methods
Three design experiments: (1) conceptual design experiment, (2) a probe study exploring AI concept sorting methods, (3) a probe study with industry practitioners evaluating risks and benefits of AI concepts through multidisciplinary collaboration.

## Main Arguments
- Most AI ethics work focuses on deployment-stage interventions; early-stage concept selection is an underexplored and high-leverage intervention point
- Practitioners can effectively assess RAI concerns when given appropriate tools and multidisciplinary framing
- Design-led approaches can surface ethical considerations that technical and business framings miss
- Low-risk, high-benefit AI concepts are identifiable early and should be prioritized in innovation pipelines

## Limitations & Critiques
Design experiments are exploratory rather than evaluative; the practitioner sample may not reflect the diversity of AI development contexts globally; the proposed approach requires organizational willingness to invest in early-stage ethics work that may not always exist.

# Mapping Value Sensitive Design onto AI for Social Good Principles

## Summary
Extends Value Sensitive Design (VSD) to address two challenges unique to machine learning AI: the opacity of learning processes (making it difficult to understand how values are embedded) and value disembodiment (AI systems adapting in ways that drift from intended values over time). Proposes a threefold modified VSD approach integrating AI4SG principles, distinguishing promoted from respected values, and extending assessment across the full technology lifecycle.

## Key Concepts
- Value Sensitive Design (VSD)
- AI for Social Good (AI4SG) principles
- Value disembodiment
- Transparency and accountability
- Full lifecycle assessment

## Theoretical Framework
VSD framework (Friedman et al.); AI4SG principles as design norms; SARS-CoV-2 contact tracing app as illustrative case for applying the modified approach.

## Methods
Conceptual/theoretical; no original empirical data; framework development illustrated through a concrete contact tracing application use case.

## Main Arguments
- ML-based AI poses two challenges to standard VSD: opacity of learning and value drift through adaptation
- AI4SG principles (fairness, transparency, accountability, etc.) can serve as design norms from which specific requirements are derived
- VSD must distinguish values the design promotes (actively advances) from those it merely respects (does not violate)
- Lifecycle monitoring is essential to catch unintended value consequences as AI systems learn and adapt post-deployment

## Limitations & Critiques
Theoretical framework not yet empirically validated; AI4SG principles remain somewhat fuzzy and contested across different stakeholder groups; the contact tracing example is illustrative rather than evaluative; operationalizing the framework in practice requires significant additional work.

# Mapping VSD onto AI for Social Good (Umbrello and van de Poel)

## Summary
Umbrello and van de Poel argue that Value Sensitive Design (VSD) requires significant modification when applied to AI — particularly machine learning — because ML systems can learn features that weren't foreseen by designers and may behave opaquely. They propose a threefold modified VSD approach: (1) integrating AI4SG (AI for Social Good) principles as concrete design norms; (2) distinguishing between values promoted vs. values respected by a design; and (3) extending VSD to the full AI lifecycle to monitor value drift. The approach is illustrated through a COVID-19 contact tracing app case.

## Key Concepts
- Value Sensitive Design (VSD)
- AI for Social Good (AI4SG) principles
- Value disembodiment in ML systems
- Transparency, explicability, accountability as AI-specific values
- Lifecycle-based value monitoring

## Theoretical Framework
Builds on Friedman et al.'s VSD methodology and extends it using AI4SG literature; distinguishes stakeholder values along "do good" vs. "do no harm" dimensions to avoid value neutrality in design.

## Methods
Theoretical/conceptual paper with applied illustration using a SARS-CoV-2 contact tracing app as a running case study to demonstrate how modified VSD maps onto design decisions.

## Main Arguments
- ML systems pose unique VSD challenges: opacity and adaptive behavior can "disembody" embedded values over time
- AI4SG principles (privacy, fairness, accountability, etc.) can serve as a pre-validated set of design norms to anchor VSD for AI
- VSD must extend past deployment — values must be monitored and the system redesigned as unintended consequences emerge
- Promoting positive outcomes requires going beyond harm avoidance to affirmatively support human flourishing

## Limitations
- AI4SG principles are themselves contested and context-dependent; mapping them to VSD may carry hidden assumptions
- Lifecycle monitoring is resource-intensive and rarely implemented in practice; paper is aspirational rather than empirically validated

Links to [[Closing the Sociotechnical Gap in AI (Sadek et al. Imperial)]] on practitioner mindset change; relates to [[Co-Producing AI Augmented Participatory Lifecycle (Mushkani et al. # Comparing Grounded Theory and Topic Modeling: Extreme Divergence or Complementary Tools? (Marquette, 2017)


## Abstract

**DOI:** [10.1002/asi.23786](https://doi.org/10.1002/asi.23786)

Researchers in information science and related areas have developed various methods for analyzing textual data, such as survey responses. This article describes the application of analysis methods from two distinct fields, one method from interpretive social science and one method from statistical machine learning, to the same survey data. The results show that the two analyses produce some similar and some complementary insights about the phenomenon of interest, in this case, nonuse of social media. We compare both the processes of conducting these analyses and the results they produce to derive insights about each method's unique advantages and drawbacks, as well as the broader roles that these methods play in the respective fields where they are often used. These insights allow us to make more informed decisions about the tradeoffs in choosing different methods for analyzing textual data. Furthermore, this comparison suggests ways that such methods might be combined in novel and compelling ways.

## Summary
This methodological paper compares grounded theory and topic modeling as approaches to qualitative data analysis, examining their epistemological assumptions, strengths, weaknesses, and appropriate contexts of use. The authors find that despite surface similarities (both generate categories from data without a priori frameworks), grounded theory and topic modeling reflect fundamentally different epistemologies: grounded theory seeks substantive theory about social processes; topic modeling seeks statistical patterns in text. The paper offers guidance for researchers choosing between and potentially combining the two approaches.

## Key Concepts
- Grounded theory (Glaser, Strauss, Charmaz)
- Topic modeling (LDA, structural topic models)
- Epistemological comparison of qualitative methods
- Theory generation vs. pattern discovery
- Mixed-methods implications

## Theoretical Framework
Research methodology meta-analysis; constructivist grounded theory (Charmaz); computational text analysis; draws on qualitative research methodology literature and natural language processing to compare the two approaches.

## Methods
Methodological review and comparison; analysis of the epistemological assumptions, procedural requirements, and output types of grounded theory and topic modeling; demonstration using a shared dataset.

## Main Arguments
- Grounded theory and topic modeling are not interchangeable despite both being inductive, data-driven approaches
- Grounded theory produces substantive theoretical accounts of social processes with interpretive richness; topic modeling produces statistical descriptions of textual patterns
- The choice between them should be driven by the research question's epistemological requirements, not by sample size or convenience
- Under appropriate conditions, the two approaches can be combined: topic modeling for initial pattern identification; grounded theory for theory-building on those patterns

Businesses dealing with educational technology are greatly engaging and spending exponentially over technologies delivering education by artificial intelligence. Such technologies generate highly interactive and deeply engaging educational experiences for the learners creating an everlasting impact. Some of the cutting-edge technologies that improve student engagement and encourage deeper connections with the educational content or the conversational assistants that interact verbally and virtually. # Media Will Never Influence Learning (Clark 1994)

## Summary
Clark's provocative 1994 paper argues that media (delivery vehicles for instruction) have no direct influence on learning — only the instructional methods embedded in media matter. His famous analogy: a truck delivers groceries but doesn't cause nutrition; what matters is the food, not the vehicle. Clark targets the tendency in educational technology research to conflate medium and method, arguing that any medium can be replaced by another if the same instructional method is implemented, yielding equivalent learning outcomes. This challenges the premise that specific technologies (film, computers, AI) are inherently superior instructional vehicles.

## Key Concepts
- Media vs. method distinction
- No-significant-difference phenomenon
- Instructional equivalence
- Confounding of medium and method in research
- Cognitive theory of instruction

## Theoretical Framework
Grounded in cognitive information processing theory; applies the logic of experimental design to critique media comparison studies; distinguishes between the symbolic systems that media can carry and the instructional events they instantiate.

## Methods
Theoretical/review paper; critical analysis of media comparison research methodology; identifies systematic confounds that bias findings in favor of new media.

## Main Arguments
- Media comparison studies routinely confound medium with method — when the same method is implemented across media, learning outcomes equate
- The "novelty effect" inflates outcomes for new media in the short term; effects dissipate as novelty wears off
- Resources should be allocated based on cost-effectiveness of different media for implementing effective methods, not on assumed inherent superiority of new technologies
- This argument directly challenges the justification for any technology integration based on the technology itself rather than on instructional design

## Limitations
- Kozma (1994) directly rebuts Clark, arguing that some media have unique symbolic and interactive capabilities that enable new instructional methods, not merely carry existing ones
- In the AI era, Clark's truck metaphor may understate how the "vehicle" (AI interaction) creates the instructional event itself
- Empirically, individual differences in modality preference complicate the method-equivalence claim

## Connections
Directly paired with [[Will Media Influence Learning Reframing the Debate (Kozma 1994)]] as classic opposing views; relates to [[Nine Ways to Reduce Cognitive Load in Multimedia (Mayer and Moreno)]] on cognitive multimedia learning; connects to [[Behaviorism Cognitivism Constructivism Compared (Ertmer and Newby)]] on instructional theory.

# Metacognitive Support Agents for Human-AI Co-Creation (Gmeiner et al. CMU)

## Summary
Gmeiner et al. explore how metacognitive support agents — AI interfaces that prompt designers to reflect on their own thinking — can improve human-AI co-creation in mechanical design tasks. Through a Wizard of Oz study with 20 designers, they find that agent-supported users produce more feasible designs and engage more deeply with problem exploration, countering the cognitive offloading tendency that GenAI workflows typically induce. The work proposes a shift from AI as output generator to AI as reflective collaborator.

## Key Concepts
- Metacognitive support agents
- Cognitive offloading (the risk of reducing designer engagement through automation)
- Intent formulation (specifying design criteria upfront for AI)
- Wizard of Oz elicitation methodology
- Reflective design practice

## Theoretical Framework
Cognitive science theories of metacognition combined with HCI research on AI-assisted design; situates the work within critiques of automation-induced deskilling and the broader discourse on human-AI collaboration.

## Methods
Wizard of Oz elicitation study with 20 mechanical designers who interacted with simulated metacognitive support agents during a 3D GenAI CAD design task; compared supported vs. non-supported users on design feasibility and process metrics.

## Main Arguments
- GenAI tools reduce cognitive engagement through offloading, which harms design quality
- Metacognitive prompting (encouraging reflection on goals and evaluation criteria) produces more feasible designs
- Different support strategies have different impacts — not all metacognitive interventions are equally effective
- AI design tools should be designed to promote thinking, not just automate output generation

## Limitations & Critiques
Wizard of Oz methodology simulates but does not fully replicate real agent behavior; the mechanical design domain may not generalize to graphic, interaction, or other creative design disciplines.

# Method in their madness: Explaining how

## Summary
This paper investigates the apparent irrationality in designers' method selection practices, arguing that what looks like "madness" in method choice is actually explicable through understanding the social, political, and contextual factors that shape design method decisions in practice. Through ethnographic observation of design teams, the authors document how designers choose methods not only for their technical utility but for their communicative, rhetorical, and political functions — methods are used to build consensus, satisfy client expectations, and signal professional competence. The paper calls for a more socially grounded account of design method use.

## Key Concepts
- Design method selection in practice
- Rhetorical and political functions of design methods
- Ethnographic design research
- Method use vs. method rationale
- Social dynamics of design practice

## Theoretical Framework
Social practice theory; ethnomethodology; design research; draws on Schön's reflective practice and organizational sociology to analyze the non-technical dimensions of design method selection.

## Methods
Ethnographic observation of design teams in professional settings; qualitative analysis of method selection decisions; interview data about designers' rationale for method choices.

## Main Arguments
- Design method selection in practice is rarely purely technical; social, political, and communicative factors consistently influence which methods designers choose
- Methods serve as boundary objects in design teams: they enable communication and coordination beyond their technical function
- The gap between espoused design methods and methods-in-use is a consistent finding in design research that existing method frameworks fail to explain
- Design education that focuses only on technical method instruction misses the social skills required for effective method deployment in practice

## Limitations & Critiques
Ethnographic study of specific design contexts; generalizability across design disciplines and organizational settings requires further investigation; the "madness" framing may be somewhat rhetorical.

# Motivation, Volition, and Performamce

## Summary
This work addresses the motivational, volitional, and performance dimensions of learning and instructional design. Drawing on Keller's ARCS model of motivational design (Attention, Relevance, Confidence, Satisfaction) and volition theory (Corno, Kuhl), the text argues that motivation—the force that initiates learning—must be distinguished from volition—the force that sustains learning through obstacles and competing demands. Instructional designers must address both, as well as the performance conditions that translate motivated, volitional effort into measurable outcomes.

## Key Concepts
- **ARCS Model**: Keller's framework for motivational design—Attention (arouse curiosity), Relevance (connect to learner goals), Confidence (build self-efficacy), Satisfaction (provide rewarding outcomes)
- **Volition**: The capacity to protect learning intentions against competing motivations and distractions; "will" rather than "want"
- **Motivational design**: Systematic approach to designing instruction that addresses motivational as well as cognitive variables
- **Self-efficacy**: Learner's belief in their capacity to succeed; a key determinant of both motivation and performance
- **Performance conditions**: Environmental, social, and physical factors that mediate the translation of motivation into achievement

## Theoretical Framework
Integrates Keller's motivational design theory with volitional control frameworks (Kuhl's action control theory, Corno's model of volition) and performance systems thinking from HPT. Positions motivation and volition as necessary but insufficient for performance; environmental conditions and skill must also be present.

## Methods
Theoretical synthesis; applies psychological models of motivation and volition to instructional design practice. Prescriptive framework for practitioners designing motivationally rich instruction.

## Main Arguments
1. Motivation is necessary but not sufficient for learning—learners must also exercise volition to sustain effort through difficulty
2. The ARCS model provides a systematic framework for designing motivational elements into instruction
3. Instructional designers who address only cognitive factors ignore the motivational and volitional variables that determine whether learning occurs
4. Performance requires attention to both internal (motivation, volition, skill) and external (environmental, social, resource) conditions

## Limitations
Motivational design research often relies on self-report measures that may not accurately reflect actual motivational states. Cross-cultural applicability of ARCS components is contested. Distinguishing motivation from volition empirically is methodologically difficult.

## Connections
- Connects to [[PRINCIPLES]] (Gagne's events of instruction, including attention and motivation)
- Relates to [[Characteristics and Evolution of Foundational Instructional]] on ADDIE-based design models
- Pairs with [[Scaffolding and Achievement in Problem-Based and Inquiry Learning]] on supporting learner persistence

## Summary

# Navigating a New Direction in HCI Education: Challenges of

## Summary
This paper examines the challenges HCI educators face as the field evolves in response to AI, examining how HCI education must adapt its curricula, methods, and pedagogical frameworks to prepare students for practice in AI-mediated technology contexts. Through surveys and interviews with HCI faculty, the authors document the challenges of teaching HCI when the fundamental nature of human-computer interaction is being transformed by AI capabilities. The paper identifies specific pedagogical adaptations and curriculum changes HCI programs are making and recommends a forward-looking HCI education framework.

## Key Concepts
- HCI education in the age of AI
- Curriculum adaptation for AI-transformed practice
- AI-mediated interaction and HCI theory
- Pedagogical challenges in evolving fields
- New HCI competencies for AI contexts

## Theoretical Framework
Design education research; HCI pedagogical frameworks; technology education theory; draws on HCI discipline history and education reform literature.

## Methods
Survey and interview study with HCI faculty across programs; qualitative analysis of curriculum adaptation strategies; thematic analysis of challenges and responses.

## Main Arguments
- AI is transforming the object of HCI study itself (what is interaction when AI mediates it?), requiring conceptual as well as practical curriculum updates
- HCI education faces a dual challenge: teaching current AI tools and practices while maintaining the discipline's foundational human-centered principles
- The rapid pace of AI change makes curriculum stability increasingly difficult; HCI programs need more modular, updateable curricula
- Students need both tool fluency and critical AI evaluation skills to navigate practice in AI-transformed technology contexts

## Limitations & Critiques
Survey-based study of faculty views may not capture student experience or actual learning outcomes; HCI education varies considerably across institutions; the rapid pace of change means recommendations may quickly become outdated.

# Navigating More-Than-Human Perspectives in HCI Education (Nilsson et al.)

## Summary
Nilsson et al. examine how HCI educators can incorporate more-than-human perspectives — posthumanist, multispecies, and ecological framings — into interaction design curricula that have historically centered human experience and needs. The paper argues that as AI, the Internet of Things, and ecological crisis reshape what HCI addresses, students must develop capacity to design with and for non-human actors, entangled systems, and uncertain futures. The authors present pedagogical approaches and student responses, finding that more-than-human framings productively destabilize students' assumptions about design's subject matter.

## Key Concepts
- More-than-human design perspectives
- Posthumanism in HCI
- Multispecies design
- Ecological design futures
- Decentering the human in interaction design education

## Theoretical Framework
Draws on posthumanist theory (Haraway, Barad), more-than-human geography, and speculative design; challenges HCI's foundational anthropocentrism and invites students to consider non-human agents, materials, and ecological systems as design stakeholders.

## Methods
Pedagogical action research; design studio courses incorporating more-than-human briefs and frameworks; thematic analysis of student project outcomes and reflections; educator reflection on pedagogical challenges.

## Main Arguments
- HCI education's dominant human-centered paradigm is insufficient for contemporary design challenges that inherently involve non-human actors (AI systems, ecosystems, microbiomes, infrastructure)
- More-than-human perspectives destabilize students' design assumptions productively — uncertainty about who/what to design for drives more reflective and ethically attentive design thinking
- Posthumanist framings do not abandon human welfare but recontextualize it within broader webs of relation — a necessary move for sustainable, equitable design
- Educators must model intellectual flexibility and genuine openness to non-anthropocentric perspectives rather than treating them as exotic add-ons

## Limitations
- Pedagogical approaches developed in a Scandinavian higher education context with specific cultural receptivity to ecological and posthumanist thinking
- Assessment challenges: more-than-human design work resists conventional evaluation criteria centered on user needs and usability

Relates to [[AI-assisted Learning in HCI Education (Heyer et al. Malmo)]] (same institutional context, Malmö); links to [[Conceptions of Design Practice (Lotsos et al. # Negotiating AI(s) Futures (Richter et al., 2025)

## Summary
Comparative stakeholder interview study examining how AI imaginaries are actively negotiated and co-constructed across institutional sectors and national contexts in the United States, China, and Germany. Challenges monolithic accounts of national AI strategies, showing that within-country variation between industry, government, academia, media, and civil society rivals cross-national differences—AI futures are multiple and contested within nations, not only between them.

## Key Concepts
- **Competing AI imaginaries**: The coexistence of contested, sector-specific visions of AI futures within and across nations
- **Stakeholder negotiation**: The active process by which different institutional actors contest and co-construct AI futures
- **Cross-national comparison**: US, China, Germany as distinct but internally heterogeneous AI imaginary spaces

## Main Arguments
1. AI imaginaries are not monolithic at the national level—within-country sectoral variation is substantial
2. Stakeholders actively contest AI futures; no single actor group controls the dominant imaginary

# Nine Ways to Reduce Cognitive Load in Multimedia (Mayer and Moreno)

## Summary
Mayer and Moreno's 2003 paper synthesizes cognitive load theory and the cognitive theory of multimedia learning (CTML) to derive nine instructional design principles for reducing cognitive overload in multimedia learning environments. They distinguish three kinds of cognitive demands — essential (intrinsic to learning the material), incidental (caused by poor design), and representational holding (managing dual-coded representations) — and for each, recommend corresponding design interventions. The nine principles span segmenting, pre-training, weeding, signaling, aligning words and pictures, eliminating redundancy, synchronizing narration with animation, individualizing, and providing learner control.

## Key Concepts
- Cognitive load theory (Sweller)
- Cognitive theory of multimedia learning (CTML)
- Essential, incidental, and representational holding load
- Nine design principles for multimedia
- Dual-channel processing (auditory + visual)

## Theoretical Framework
Grounds in Baddeley's working memory model (dual phonological/visual channels) and Sweller's cognitive load theory; extends CTML to distinguish multiple types of load and prescribe design solutions for each type.

## Methods
Theoretical synthesis; reviews empirical studies validating each of the nine principles; draws on Mayer's extensive laboratory research program using narrated animations as the primary experimental paradigm.

## Main Arguments
- Cognitive overload is the primary cause of ineffective multimedia learning — not media choice per se
- Incidental load (irrelevant design elements, redundant text/narration, unsynchronized materials) can and should be eliminated through principled design
- Essential load can be managed through segmenting complex content and providing pre-training on component elements
- Representational holding load (maintaining mental representations across modalities) can be reduced through spatial and temporal contiguity of words and pictures

## Limitations
- Most empirical work uses controlled lab studies with narrated animations; generalizability to complex, real-world multimedia environments is contested
- Principles can conflict in practice (e.g., individualization vs. streamlining)
- Later research has complicated the redundancy principle in specific contexts

## Connections
Directly applies [[Behaviorism Cognitivism Constructivism Compared (Ertmer and Newby)]] cognitive frameworks to design; relates to [[Will Media Influence Learning Reframing the Debate (Kozma 1994)]] and [[Media Will Never Influence Learning (Clark 1994)]] on media and learning debate; informs instructional design in AI-assisted learning contexts.

# Optimizing Design Education Using Artificial Intelligence (IJHSES, 2025)

## Summary
Proposes and tests an AI-based design education framework combining Outcome-Based Education (OBE), an intelligent color platform (Coolors), and a Backpropagation (BP) neural network to optimize color composition teaching for visual communication design students. A quasi-experimental study with 120 students shows statistically significant improvements over traditional methods.

## Key Concepts
- Outcome-Based Education (OBE)
- Backpropagation (BP) neural network
- Intelligent color platform (Coolors)
- Predictive analytics in education
- Color composition pedagogy

## Theoretical Framework
OBE as a closed-loop instructional model with competency-driven objectives; BP neural network as predictive analytics layer; integrates design education theory with machine learning.

## Methods
Quasi-experimental design; 120 visual communication design students divided into experimental (OBE + AI tools) and control (traditional instruction) groups; quantitative comparison of design project scores and theoretical exam performance; post-study survey on student approval.

## Main Arguments
- Experimental group scored 7.83 points higher on design projects and 6.27 points higher on theoretical exams compared to controls (p < 0.01)
- BP neural network achieved 2.62% mean prediction error in learning outcome forecasting
- 71.7% of students approved the digital tool integration
- The framework demonstrates that AI-driven predictive analytics can personalize competency-based creative education

## Limitations & Critiques
Single institution in China; narrow focus on color composition limits generalizability to other design competencies; quasi-experimental design cannot fully control confounds; high specialization of the Coolors platform may not transfer to other design domains.

## Summary
Pershing's foundational chapter on Human Performance Technology (HPT) defines the field, traces its historical origins in behavioral psychology and systems thinking, and presents the core HPT framework that distinguishes performance problems from training solutions. The chapter establishes that HPT is not synonymous with training but encompasses the full range of interventions — from job redesign and incentive systems to communication improvements — needed to close performance gaps. It argues for a systematic, evidence-based approach to workplace performance improvement.

## Key Concepts
- Human Performance Technology (HPT) definition and scope
- Performance gap analysis (actual vs. desired performance)
- Training vs. non-training interventions
- Behavioral and systems thinking foundations
- ISPI (International Society for Performance Improvement) standards

## Theoretical Framework
Behavioral systems approach; draws on B.F. Skinner's behavioral analysis, Gilbert's behavioral engineering model, and systems theory to frame performance improvement as an engineering problem requiring systematic analysis before solution selection.

## Methods
Conceptual framework development; historical review of HPT's intellectual origins; descriptive overview of the HPT model and its application phases.

## Main Arguments
- Most workplace performance problems are not caused by lack of training; environmental and systemic factors are often more powerful
- HPT requires front-end analysis to correctly identify the cause of performance gaps before prescribing interventions
- The field's core value proposition is return on investment: selecting cost-effective interventions that close the performance gap
- Ethical HPT practice requires transparency, competence, and alignment with organizational and individual values

## Limitations & Critiques
Critics argue HPT's behavioral foundations undervalue intrinsic motivation and creativity; the field's corporate orientation can deprioritize worker wellbeing in favor of productivity metrics.

# Perceptions of GenAI in Creative Industries: Scoping Review (Tsao et al.)

## Summary
Tsao et al. conduct a scoping review of empirical research on how creative industry professionals — in design, advertising, film, music, and fashion — perceive and respond to generative AI tools. Synthesizing findings across 40+ studies, the review identifies consistent patterns: initial curiosity followed by concerns about professional identity, quality of AI-generated work, intellectual property, and the devaluation of human creative labor. The review maps the landscape of attitudes from enthusiastic integration to active resistance, organized by creative domain and professional role.

## Key Concepts
- Creative industry professional perceptions of GenAI
- Professional identity threat and adaptation
- Intellectual property and AI-generated creative work
- Human creative labor devaluation
- Scoping review methodology

## Theoretical Framework
Uses scoping review methods (Arksey and O'Malley); organizes findings through job crafting and professional identity frameworks; considers threat appraisal theory to explain the range of defensive and adaptive responses to GenAI.

## Methods
Systematic scoping review; database searches across multiple disciplines; inclusion/exclusion criteria focused on empirical studies of professional perceptions; thematic synthesis across creative domains.

## Main Arguments
- Creative professionals across domains share a cluster of concerns about GenAI: authenticity, skill devaluation, attribution, and displacement — though the relative salience varies by domain
- Design and advertising professionals show more pragmatic adoption than fine art or music professionals, whose identity is more deeply tied to the creative act itself
- IP and attribution concerns are nearly universal among professional creatives, even among those who actively use GenAI tools
- Resistance to GenAI is not uniform technophobia — it is often a principled response to perceived threats to craft, livelihood, and cultural value

## Limitations
- Rapidly evolving landscape; perceptions reported in studies from 2022-2024 may already be outdated as tools and industry norms evolve
- Publication bias toward English-language, Western creative industries contexts
